\label{thm:no-gain}
Suppose $(T,R)$ is fully observed, $P_{R\mid T}$ is unrestricted,
and $\psi(P)=\psi(P_T)$ is a scalar pathwise differentiable parameter with marginal IF $\varphi_T$.
Then
$ \varphi_{\mathrm{joint}}(T,R)=\varphi_T(T). $

Assumption~\ref{ass:eif-gain-primitives} holds.
For $\ell=jk\in\mathcal J$, $M_{\ell,i}(t)=N_{\ell,i}(t)-\int_0^tY_{j,i}(u)\,dA_{\ell}(u)$ is square integrable.
Write $q_j(u)=E\{Y_j(u)\}=P_j(u-)G(u-)$, $j=0,1$.

\item\label{ajmain:support}
  With $\mathcal T_j=\{u\in(0,\tau]:q_j(u)>0\}$, the infimum of $q_j$ on every compact subset of $\mathcal T_j$ is positive,
  and $\int_0^\tau I\{q_{j(\ell)}(u)=0\}\,dA_\ell(u)=0$.
\item\label{ajmain:inverse}
  For each $\ell$,
\[
   V_\ell^\textsf{AJ}(\tau)= \int_{(0,\tau]}\frac{I\{q_{j(\ell)}(u)>0\}}{q_{j(\ell)}(u)}\,dA_\ell(u)<\infty.
\]
\end{enumerate}

title: Assumption
body_md:
\label{ass:main-transition-martingale-linearization}
For a deterministic sequence $a_N\downarrow0$, suppose that for every fold $k$, relative to the training-sample calendar-time filtration $\mathbb F_{-k}=\{\mathcal F_{-k}(u):0\le u\le\tau\}$,
\begin{align*}
  D_{k,\ell}(u\mid x)
  =
  U_{k,\ell}(u\mid x)+R_{k,\ell}(u\mid x),
  \qquad \ell\in\mathcal J,
\end{align*}
where $U_{k,\ell}(\cdot\mid x)$ is a square-integrable $\mathbb F_{-k}$-martingale and the stochastic Fubini interchanges below are valid.
The process $e_{G,-k}(u,x)$ is left-continuous and $\mathbb F_{-k}$-predictable.
For every bounded $\mathbb F_{-k}$-predictable multiplier $z$, write
$
\|z\|_{2,\infty}
=
\left[
P_X\left\{\sup_{0\le u\le\tau}|z(u,X)|^2\right\}
\right]^{1/2},
$
and define
\begin{align*}
  \mathcal U_{k,z}(t)
  &=
  \sum_{\ell\in\mathcal J}
  P_X\int_0^t
  L_{\ell,0}(u,X)z(u,X)\,dU_{k,\ell}(u\mid X),
\\
  \mathcal R_{k,z}
  &=
  \sum_{\ell\in\mathcal J}
  P_X\int_0^\tau
  L_{\ell,0}(u,X)z(u,X)\,dR_{k,\ell}(u\mid X).
\end{align*}
There are random variables $C_{k,N}=O_p(1)$, uniformly over the fixed number of folds, such that
$
  \langle\mathcal U_{k,z}\rangle(\tau)
  \le C_{k,N}a_N^2\|z\|_{2,\infty}^2,
$ and $ 
  |\mathcal R_{k,z}|
  \le C_{k,N}a_N\|z\|_{2,\infty}.
$

title: Definition
body_md:
A function $\phi\in L^2_0(P)$ is an influence function (IF) for the parameter $\psi(P)$ at $P$,
relative to a model $\mathcal{M}\equiv\{ P \}$, if:
for every regular one-dimensional submodel
$\{  P^{(\epsilon)} \}_{\epsilon\in(-\eta,\eta)}\subset\mathcal{M}$ with a score function
$s(t,r)\equiv\partial_\epsilon\log f^{(\epsilon)}(t,r)\big|_{\epsilon=0} \in L^2_0(P)$,
the pathwise derivative of $\psi$ at $P$ is given by the inner product of the score with $\phi$:
\begin{align*}
  \partial_\epsilon \psi(P^{(\epsilon)})\big|_{\epsilon=0}
  =
  E \{\phi(T,R) s(T,R)\} , \qquad\forall s\in\mathcal{T}_P(\mathcal{M}).
\end{align*}
An IF $\phi\equiv\phi_{P}(t,r)$ is determined jointly by $\psi$ and $\mathcal{M}$, and is an $L^2_0(P)$ function that varies with $P\in\mathcal{M}$.
Geometrically, $\phi_P$ is the $L^2(P)$ gradient of the functional $\psi$ on $\mathcal{M}$.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
The semiparametric efficiency bound for $\psi(P)$ relative to $\mathcal{M}$ is
$\inf_{\phi \in \textsf{IF}(\psi,P;\mathcal{M})} E \phi^2(T,R),$
where $\textsf{IF}(\psi,P;\mathcal{M})$ is the set of all influence functions.
The IF that achieves the bound is called the efficient influence function (EIF).
Geometrically, the EIF is the $L^2(P)$ projection of any IF onto $\mathcal{T}_P(\mathcal{M})$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We use regular parametric submodels in a dominated model.
Let $\mathcal{T}_R$ be the nuisance tangent space corresponding to perturbations of $P_{R|T}$.
Since the conditional law $P_{R|T}$ is unrestricted,
$$
\mathcal{T}_R = \big\{ s(t,r)\in L^2(P) \ ;\ P[s(T,R)\,|\,T]=0 \text{ a.s. } \big\} .
$$
The parameter $\psi(P)$ is invariant under perturbations in $\mathcal{T}_R$.
Its EIF $\phi_P(t,r)$ therefore satisfies $E[\phi_P(T,R) s(T,R)] = 0$ for all $s \in \mathcal{T}_R$,
and hence $\phi_P\in\mathcal{T}^\perp_R$.
The orthogonal complement of $\mathcal{T}_R$ in $L^2_0(P_{T,R})$ consists of the mean-zero functions of the marginal variable with law $P_T$:
$$
\mathcal{T}^\perp_R = \big\{ g(T)\in L^2(P_T)\ ;\ Eg(T) = 0 \big\} .
$$
Consequently, the EIF in $\mathcal{M}$ for $P_{T,R}$ agrees with the EIF in the reduced model $\mathcal{M}_0$ for $P_T$:
$\phi_{P_T}(T)\equiv \phi_{P_{T,R}}(T,R)$ a.s..
The efficiency bounds for $\psi(P_{T,R})$ in $\mathcal{M}$ and $\mathcal{M}_0$ thus coincide.

label: lem:martingale-representation
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:martingale-representation}
We ignore censoring $C$ in this lemma, and assume that $\mathcal{F}^\bullet$ is generated only by $N^*_T(t)$.
The tangent space $\mathcal{T}_P\equiv\big\{ g\in L^2(P,\mathcal{F}^\bullet) \ ;\ \mathbb{E}g(T)=0 \big\}$
of density score functions has the following characterization.
Define
\[
\mathcal{T}^M_P=
  \bigg\{
    \int_0^\infty h(t) \;\mathrm{d} M^\bullet_T(t)
    \ ;\
    \mathbb{E}h^2(T)=\int_0^\infty h^2(t) S(t) \lambda(t) \;\mathrm{d}t <\infty
  \bigg\} .
\]
Then $\mathcal{T}^M_P=\{g(T)\ ;\ g\in \mathcal{T}_P\}$.
In particular, the full-data IF of $\theta(P)$ can be expressed as:
\begin{equation} \label{eq:IF-M-star}
  \phi^\bullet(T)
  = I(T>\tau) - \theta
  = \int_0^\infty \big\{ I(s>\tau)-v(s)\big\} \;\mathrm{d} M^\bullet_T(s)
  = \int_0^\tau \;\mathrm{d} M^\bullet_\theta(s) .
\end{equation}

title: Proof
body_md:
For $h\in L^2(P_T)$, the martingale isometry and Fubini's theorem give
\[
  E\left\{\int_0^\infty h(t)\,\mathrm{d}M_T^\bullet(t)\right\}^{2}
  =\int_0^\infty h(t)^2S(t)\lambda(t)\,\mathrm{d}t
  =Eh(T)^2<\infty.
\]
The integral is $T$-measurable and has mean zero, proving the first inclusion.
Conversely, for $g\in\mathcal T_P$, the closed martingale
$M_g(t):=E\{g(T)\mid\mathcal F_t^\bullet\}$ is square-integrable, with terminal value $g(T)$.
The point-process representation theorem \cite{jacod1975multivariate} gives
$M_g(t)=\int_0^tH(s)\,\mathrm{d} M_T^\bullet(s)$.
Before the single jump, the event history specifies only that $T\ge t$;
thus $H(t)=h(t)Y^*(t)$ for a deterministic $h$.
Since $M_T^\bullet$ has no increments after $T$, this proves the reverse inclusion.
The isometry also gives $Eh(T)^2=Eg(T)^2<\infty$.

To identify $h$, put $V(t):=E\{g(T)\,|\,T>t\}$.
Strictly prior to $T$, $M_g(t)=V(t)$; at $T$, $M_g$ has a jump and takes the value $M_g(T)=g(T)$.
Absolute continuity of the event-time law makes $V$ continuous on the survival support,
so $\Delta M_g(T)=g(T)-V(T)=h(T)$.
For $g(t)=\phi^*(t)=I(t>\tau)-\theta$, the conditional survival probability
$v(t)$ defined above therefore gives $h(t)=I(t>\tau)-v(t)$.
It equals $-v(t)$ on $[0,\tau]$ and zero after $\tau$, proving \eqref{eq:IF-M-star}.
The hazard-score interpretation of $h$ follows from the likelihood differentiation in \eqref{eq:hazard-score}.

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $F=(T,C)$ denote the full data, with law $P_F$, and let $P_V$ denote the observed-data law.
The full-data factorization is
$P_F(\mathrm{d}t,\mathrm{d}c)=f_{T}(t)\mathrm{d}t\times f_{C}(c)\mathrm{d}c .$
The probability of observing $T$, conditional on $T$, is $P\{\Delta=1\,|\,T\}=P\{C>T\,|\,T\}=G(T).$
Thus $P\{\Delta=0\,|\,T\}=1-G(T)$, and the observed-data law is the continuous--discrete mixture
$$
  P_V(\mathrm{d}t,\delta)
  =
  \Big\{ f_T(t)G(t)\mathrm{d}t \Big\}^\delta \cdot
  \bigg\{ I_\emptyset(t)\int_0^\infty [1-G(s)] f_T(s) \; \mathrm{d}s \bigg\}^{1-\delta} .
$$

Fix a full-data score $s_F(t,c)=s_T(t)+s_C(c)$ for $P_F$,
where $s_T(t)=\partial_\epsilon\big|_{\epsilon=0}\log f^{(\epsilon)}_T(t)$,
and $s_C(c)=\partial_\epsilon\big|_{\epsilon=0}\log f^{(\epsilon)}_C(c)$
correspond to the perturbation $f^{(\epsilon)}_{T}(t)f^{(\epsilon)}_{C}(c)$ of $P_F$.
The induced observed-data score $s_V$ is obtained by differentiating each component of the mixture.
When $\Delta=0$,
\[
s_V(\emptyset,0)=\partial_\epsilon\big|_{\epsilon=0}
  \log \int I(c<t) \;\mathrm{d}P^{(\epsilon)}_{T,C}(t,c)
  =
  \int_0^\infty \int_0^t \big\{s_T(t)+s_C(c)\big\} \frac{I(c<t) f_{T,C}(t,c)}{P\{C<T\}} \;\mathrm{d}c \;\mathrm{d}t ,
\]
and, when $\Delta=1$,
\begin{align*}
s_V(t,1)
  =
  \partial_\epsilon\big|_{\epsilon=0}
  \log f^{(\epsilon)}_T(t) G^{(\epsilon)}(t)
  &=
  s_T(t) + \frac{1}{G(t)} \int_t^\infty s_C(c) f_C(c) \;\mathrm{d} c
  .
\end{align*}
Thus $s_V(t,\delta)= L[s_F]\coloneqq E[s_F(T,C)\,|\,V=(t,\delta)]$ is the conditional expectation of the $P_F$ score,
and the induced tangent space at $P_V$ is
\begin{align}
  \mathcal{T}_V
  &=
  \Big\{ s_V(T^\Delta,\Delta) = E[s_T(T)+s_C(C)| T^\Delta,\Delta ]
  \ ;\
  s_T\in L^2_0(P_T),\ s_C\in L^2_0(P_C) \Big\}, \notag \\
\label{eq:score-SV}
  s_V(t,\delta)
  &=
  \delta\cdot \big[s_T(t) + \tilde s_C(t)\big] + (1-\delta)\cdot E[s_T(T)+s_C(C) \,|\, C<T]
\end{align}
where $\tilde s_C(t) =  E[s_C(C) \,|\, C>t] $.
The missing-not-at-random mechanism $\Delta$ gives $s_V(\emptyset,0)\neq 0$.

The functional
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:observed-law-functional}
  \theta(P_V)
  :=
  \int \frac{\delta I(t>\tau)}{G(t)} \;\mathrm{d}P_V(t,\delta)
  =
  \int \frac{I(t>\tau)}{G(t)} f_T(t)G(t) \;\mathrm{d}t
\end{equation}
identifies $\theta(P_F)$. Along a perturbation $P^{(\epsilon)}_F$ with score $s_F$,
\begin{align*}
\partial_\epsilon\theta(P^{(\epsilon)}_V)
  &=
  \int \frac{\delta I(t>\tau)}{G(t)} \{ s_T(t)+\tilde s_C(t) \} \;\mathrm{d}P_V(t,\delta)
    +
    \int \frac{\delta I(t>\tau)}{G(t)} \{ -\tilde s_C(t) \}  \;\mathrm{d}P_V(t,\delta) .
\end{align*}
The $\tilde s_C$ terms cancel. Under the maintained independence assumption,
$\theta(P_V)$ is therefore invariant under perturbations of $G$.

The EIF of $\theta(P_V)$ is a $P_V$-score of the form
$\phi_V(t,\delta)\equiv\delta\cdot \phi_T(t) + (1-\delta)\cdot \phi_0$
for a $P_T$-score $\phi_T$ and $\phi_0\coloneqq{E}[\phi_T(T) \,|\, C<T]$.
Iterated expectation gives $P_V\phi_V=P_T\phi_T=0$.
On $\mathcal{T}_V$, the $L^2(P_V)$ inner product of pairs of scores of the form \eqref{eq:score-SV} is
\begin{align} \label{eq:observed-law-product}
  \langle u_V, v_V \rangle_{P_V}
  &=
  \int \big\{u_T(t)+\tilde u_C(t)\big\}\big\{v_T(t)+\tilde v_C(t)\big\} f_T(t) G(t) \;\mathrm{d} t
  \\
  &\hspace{1cm} + P\{C<T\} \cdot {E}[u_F(T,C)\,|\,C<T]\cdot {E}[v_F(T,C)\,|\,C<T] . \notag
\end{align}
The score components $L[s_T]$ and $L[s_C]$ are not orthogonal.
In particular, the only $s\in\mathcal{T}_V$ orthogonal to $E[s_C(C)\,|\,V]$ is the zero score.
Thus the missing-not-at-random model requires knowledge of $G$ external to the observed $V$ data for identification.

We now restrict attention to $\mathcal{T}_T$, the perturbations of $P_T$. We seek
$\phi_V\in\mathcal{T}_V$ of the form
$\phi_V(t,\delta)=\delta \phi_T(t) + (1-\delta)\phi_0$,
$\phi_0 = \mathbb{E}[\phi_T(T)\,|\,C<T]$, $\phi_T\in L^2_0(P_T)$,
such that, for every $s_T\in \mathcal{T}_F$ inducing \eqref{eq:score-SV},
\[
  P_F\{\phi_Fs_T\} = P_V\{\phi_Vs_V\} ,
  \qquad \forall  s_T\in\mathcal{T}_T,
  \qquad \phi_F(t)=I(t>\tau)-\theta .
\]
The form \eqref{eq:score-SV} does not require $\phi_V$ to be the image of
$\phi_F$; in particular, $\phi_T$ need not equal $\phi_F$.
By \cref{eq:observed-law-functional},
\begin{equation} \label{eq:IF-phiF}
  P_F\{\phi_Fs_F\}
  =
   \int \phi_F(t) s_T(t) \;\mathrm{d}P_F
  =
  \int \frac{\phi_F(t)}{G(t)} s_T(t) G(t) \;\mathrm{d}P_T(t)
\end{equation}
whereas the inner product in \cref{eq:observed-law-product} gives
\begin{align}
  P_V\{\phi_Vs_V\}
  &=
  \int \phi_T(t) s_T(t) G(t)  \;\mathrm{d}P_T(t)
  + \phi_0 \cdot \int
  s_T(t)[1-G(t)]
  \;\mathrm{d}P_T(t) \notag \\
\label{eq:IF-phiV}
  &=
  \int
    \Big\{ \phi_T(t)G(t)
    +
    \phi_0(1-G(t))
    \Big\} s_T(t)
  \;\mathrm{d}P_T(t),
  \qquad\qquad \forall  s_T\in\mathcal{T}_T.
\end{align}
Matching the integrands in \cref{eq:IF-phiF} and \cref{eq:IF-phiV} yields
$\phi_F(t) = \Big\{ \phi_T(t)G(t) + \phi_0 (1-G(t)) \Big\}$, equivalently $\phi_T(t) = \frac{\phi_F(t)}{G(t)} - \frac{\phi_0(1-G(t))}{G(t)}$.
Substituting the preceding expression for $\phi_T$ into
$\phi_0=E\{\phi_T(T)\mid C<T\}$ yields
\[
\phi_0\int\frac{1-G(t)}{G(t)}\,\mathrm{d}P_T(t)
=\int\phi_F(t)\frac{1-G(t)}{G(t)}\,\mathrm{d}P_T(t).
\]
Thus $\phi_0=\int\phi_F(t)\omega(t)\,\mathrm{d}P_T(t)$,
where $\omega(t)\coloneqq\frac{(1-G(t))/G(t)}{\int(1-G(t))/G(t)\,\mathrm{d}P_T(t)}$.
The centering constant is thus a tilted expectation of the full-data IF.
Substitution into the expression for $\phi_T$ gives
\begin{align}
  \phi_T(t)
  &=
  \frac{1}{G(t)} \big\{ \phi_F(t) - \phi_0(1-G(t)) \big\}
  =
  \frac{1}{G(t)} \big\{ \phi_F(t) - \phi_0 \big\} + \phi_0
  \notag \\
  \phi_V(t,\delta)
  &=
  \delta \phi_T(t) + (1-\delta)\phi_0
  =
  \frac{\delta}{G(t)} \big\{ \phi_F(t)-\phi_0\big\} + \phi_0
  =
  \frac{\delta}{G(t)}\phi_F(t) + \Big\{ 1-\frac{\delta}{G(t)} \Big\}\phi_0
  \notag \\
  &=
  \phi_F(t) + \Big\{ \frac{\delta}{G(t)}-1 \Big\} \big\{ \phi_F(t)-\phi_0\big\} .
  \label{eq:IF-phiVortho}
\end{align}
Finally, the decomposition in \cref{eq:IF-phiVortho} is orthogonal:
conditioning the product of its two terms on $T$ gives zero because
$E\{\Delta/G(T)-1\mid T\}=0$.

label: eq:hazard-score
title: Proof
body_md:
Let $F=(T,C)$ and $O=(\tilde T,\Delta)$, and work under \Cref{ass:time-reg,ass:C-ignore}.
For this proof, let $\mathcal F_t^\bullet=\sigma\{N_T^*(s),N_C^*(s):0\le s\le t\}$ be the joint full-data filtration,
and write $\bm N(t)=(N(t),N_C(t))$ and $Y(t)=I(\tilde T\ge t)$.
The full-data and observed-data likelihoods, \cite{jacod1975multivariate}, are
\begin{align*}
  L^\bullet(\bm N^*)
  &=
  \bigg\{\prod_{0<t\le\tau_0}\lambda(t)^{\mathrm{d}N^*_T(t)} \lambda_C(t)^{\mathrm{d}N^*_C(t)}\bigg\}
  \exp\bigg(-\int_0^{\tau_0}\{\lambda(t)Y^*_T+\lambda_C(t)Y^*_C(t)\}\,\mathrm{d}t\bigg)
  \\
  L^\circ(\bm N)
  &=
  \bigg\{\prod_{0<t\le\tau_0}\lambda(t)^{\mathrm{d}N(t)} \lambda_C(t)^{\mathrm{d}N_C(t)}\bigg\}
  \exp\bigg(-\int_0^{\tau_0}\{\lambda(t)+\lambda_C(t)\}Y(t)\,\mathrm{d}t\bigg).
\end{align*}
For a regular perturbation of the death hazard, define
\begin{equation} \label{eq:hazard-score}
  h(t)\coloneqq\partial_\epsilon\big|_{\epsilon=0}\log\lambda^{(\epsilon)}(t).
\end{equation}
Differentiating the log-likelihood gives the death score
$s^\circ(O)=\partial_\epsilon\log L^{\circ(\epsilon)}(\bm N) =\int_0^{\tau_0}h(t)\,\mathrm{d}M^\circ(t)$.
The corresponding full-data score is $s^\bullet(F)=\int_0^{\tau_0}h(t)\,\mathrm{d}M^\bullet(t)$;
the same calculation applies to the censoring hazard.
Thus the full-data and observed-data tangent spaces have the decompositions
$\mathcal T^\bullet=\mathcal T^\bullet_T\otimes\mathcal T^\bullet_C$ and
$\mathcal T^\circ=\mathcal T^\circ_T\otimes\mathcal T^\circ_C$, respectively, with
\[
\mathcal T^\circ
=\bigg\{
  \int_0^{\tau_0}h_T(t)\,\mathrm{d}M^\circ(t)
  +\int_0^{\tau_0}h_C(t)\,\mathrm{d}M_C^\circ(t) \;:\;
  h_T\in L^2(P_T),\ h_C\in L^2(P_C)
\bigg\}.
\]
The score operator $L[s^\bullet]=E\{ s^\bullet(F)\,|\,O\}$ replaces each full-data martingale integral by its observed-data counterpart.
Absence of simultaneous event and censoring jumps makes the two score components orthogonal.
Perturbing the censoring law does not change the target, although the influence function may depend on that law.

Differentiating $\theta=S(\tau)$ along a death-hazard perturbation gives
\begin{equation} \label{eq:IF-h-product}
  \left.\partial_\epsilon\theta(P^{\circ(\epsilon)})\right|_{\epsilon=0}
  =-S(\tau)\int_0^\tau h(t)\lambda(t)\,\mathrm{d}t.
\end{equation}
For two event-hazard scores, the martingale isometry gives
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:M-isometry}
  E\big\{s^\circ_1(O)s^\circ_2(O)\big\}
  =E\int_0^{\tau_0}h_1(t)h_2(t)Y(t)\lambda(t)\,\mathrm{d}t.
\end{equation}
Since $E\{Y(t)\}=S(t)G(t)$ and $v(t)=S(\tau)/S(t)$ for $t\le\tau$,
matching \eqref{eq:IF-h-product} with \eqref{eq:M-isometry} gives
$b(t)=-v(t)/G(t)$ on $[0,\tau]$ and zero thereafter.
This representer lies in the event-score tangent space and is orthogonal to the censoring scores.
Hence
\begin{equation} \label{eq:IF-Va-M}
  \phi^\circ(O)=\int_0^\tau\frac{-v(t)}{G(t)}\,\mathrm{d}M^\circ(t)
  =\int_0^\tau\frac{Y_C^*(t)}{G(t)}\,\mathrm{d}M_\theta^\bullet(t),
\end{equation}
where the last equality uses stopping at censoring and \eqref{eq:M-theta-bullet}.

For the augmentation representations, put $U(t)=I(C>t)/G(t)$ and $V(t)=M_\theta^\bullet(t)$.
The product rule is
\begin{equation} \label{eq:UV-integration}
  \mathrm{d}[UV](t)=U(t-)\mathrm{d}V(t)+V(t-)\mathrm{d}U(t)
  +\mathrm{d}[U,V](t).
\end{equation}
Here
$\mathrm{d}U(t)=I(C\ge t)\,\mathrm{d}\Lambda_C(t)/G(t) -\mathrm{d}N_C^*(t)/G(t)=-\mathrm{d}M_C^\bullet(t)/G(t)$ and
$\mathrm{d}V(t)=-v(t)\,\mathrm{d}M^\bullet(t)$.
The cross-variation vanishes because the event and censoring processes have no simultaneous jumps.
Therefore
\begin{equation} \label{eq:UV-formula}
  \mathrm{d}\left\{\frac{I(C>t)M_\theta^\bullet(t)}{G(t)}\right\}
  =\frac{I(C\ge t)}{G(t)}\,\mathrm{d}M_\theta^\bullet(t)
  -\frac{M_\theta^\bullet(t-)}{G(t)}\,\mathrm{d}M_C^\bullet(t).
\end{equation}
The initial product is zero. At $\tilde T\wedge\tau$, it is
$I(C>\tilde T\wedge\tau)\phi^*(\tilde T)/G(\tilde T\wedge\tau)$:
the indicator removes the censored cases in which the score martingale has not yet reached its terminal value.
Integrating \eqref{eq:UV-formula} to this endpoint and setting
$\Delta_{C,\tau}=I(C>\tilde T\wedge\tau)$ yields
\begin{equation} \label{eq:IF-circ-two}
  \phi^\circ(O)=\frac{\Delta_{C,\tau}}{G(\tilde T\wedge\tau)}\phi^*(\tilde T)
  +\int_0^{\tilde T\wedge\tau}
  \frac{M_\theta^\bullet(t-)}{G(t)}\,\mathrm{d}M_C^\bullet(t).
\end{equation}
The stopped interval of integration is essential for $\mathcal{F}^\circ$-measurability:
after $T$ the centered score martingale is constant but need not be zero,
so the full-data censoring integral without stopping need not be a function of $O$.

We develop a second augmented IF representation.
Use the product identity \eqref{eq:UV-integration} with
$V(t)=M_\theta^\bullet(t)+\theta=v(t)Y_T^*(t+)$.
The differentials are unchanged, while the boundary products at $0$ and
$\tau$ are $\theta$ and $I(C>\tau)I(T>\tau)/G(\tau)$.
Thus
\begin{equation} \label{eq:UV-MMC}
  \frac{I(C>\tau)I(T>\tau)}{G(\tau)}-\theta
  =\int_0^\tau\frac{-v(t)Y_C^*(t)}{G(t)}\,\mathrm{d}M^\bullet(t)
  -\int_0^\tau\frac{v(t)Y_T^*(t)}{G(t)}\,\mathrm{d}M_C^\bullet(t).
\end{equation}
Substitution of \eqref{eq:IF-Va-M} gives
\[
  \phi^\circ(O)=\frac{I(\tilde T>\tau)}{G(\tau)}-\theta
  +\int_0^\tau\frac{M_\theta^\bullet(t-)+\theta}{G(t)}\,\mathrm{d}M_C^\circ(t).
\]
Here $M_\theta^\bullet(t-)+\theta=v(t)Y_T^*(t)$ vanishes after death,
which permits the observed censoring martingale increments on $[0,\tau]$.

Finally, \eqref{eq:M-isometry} and independence of $T,C$ give
\[
\mathbb V\{\phi^\circ(O)\}
=\int_0^\tau\frac{v(t)^2S(t)G(t)\lambda(t)}{G(t)^2}\,\mathrm{d}t
=\theta^2\int_0^\tau\frac{\lambda(t)}{S(t)G(t)}\,\mathrm{d}t.
\]
The two martingale terms in \eqref{eq:UV-MMC} are orthogonal, and the
isometry gives the censoring term variance
$\theta^2\int_0^\tau\lambda_C(t)/\{S(t)G(t)\}\,\mathrm{d}t$.
Since $P(\tilde T>\tau)=S(\tau)G(\tau)$, the variance of its left side is
$\theta/G(\tau)-\theta^2$.
Subtracting proves the second expression:
\[
  \mathbb V\{\phi^\circ(O)\}
  =\frac{\theta}{G(\tau)}-\theta^2
  -\theta^2\int_0^\tau\frac{\lambda_C(t)}{S(t)G(t)}\,\mathrm{d}t.
\]

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:rmst-hazard-derivative}
Let $A,B\in\mathscr A_{\tau}$ and $D=B-A$.  Write
$M_{\tau}(A):=\mu_A(\tau).$
Throughout the paper,
$\dot\mu_{\tau,A}[D]$ denotes the first-order pathwise derivative of the
deterministic RMST map $M_{\tau}$ at the hazard triplet $A$, evaluated in
the signed finite-variation direction $D$.  Equivalently, if
$A_\varepsilon=A+\varepsilon D$ is an admissible finite-variation path for small
$\varepsilon$, then
$\dot\mu_{\tau,A}[D] =\left.\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}M_{\tau}(A_\varepsilon) \right|_{\varepsilon=0}.$
The paper uses the following explicit Stieltjes representation as the definition of
this derivative for all signed finite-variation directions $D$:
\begin{align}
\label{eq:rmst-pathwise-derivative}
\dot\mu_{\tau,A}[D]
&=
\int_{(0,\tau]}
P^A_0(u-)
\{V^A_1(u,\tau)-V^A_0(u,\tau)\}
\,dD_{01}(u) \\
&\quad-
\int_{(0,\tau]}
P^A_0(u-)V^A_0(u,\tau)\,dD_{02}(u) \notag \\
&\quad-
\int_{(0,\tau]}
P^A_1(u-)V^A_1(u,\tau)\,dD_{12}(u). \notag
\end{align}
Thus $\dot\mu_{\tau,A}[D]$ is a scalar linear functional of the three signed
hazard increments $(dD_{01},dD_{02},dD_{12})$.  It is the linear term in the RMST
expansion
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:rmst-first-order-expansion}
\mu_B(\tau)-\mu_A(\tau)=\dot\mu_{\tau,A}[D]+r_{A,B},
\end{equation}
with remainder satisfying
$|r_{A,B}|\le \tau\omega_{\mathrm{PI}}(A,B)$.
Also,
$|\mu_B(\tau)-\mu_A(\tau)| \le 2\tau\kappa_{\mathrm{PI}}(A,B).$

label: lem:aj-jump-regularity
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:aj-jump-regularity}
Under Assumptions~\ref{ass:time-reg}, \ref{ass:C-ignore}, \ref{ass:Markov-state}, and~\ref{ass:aj-main-integrated}, let $R_i$ be the latent recurrence time and $T_i$
the latent terminal event time.  Define the transition times
\[
S_{01,i}=\begin{cases}R_i, & R_i<T_i,\\ \infty, & R_i\ge T_i,\end{cases}
\qquad
S_{02,i}=\begin{cases}T_i, & T_i<R_i,\\ \infty, & T_i\ge R_i,\end{cases}
\qquad
S_{12,i}=\begin{cases}T_i, & R_i<T_i,\\ \infty, & R_i\ge T_i.\end{cases}
\]
Then the following hold.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textnormal{(\roman*)}]
\item The true transition compensators are continuous:
$\Delta A_{\ell,0}(u)=0, \qquad 0<u\le\tau, \qquad \ell\in\mathcal J .$
\item The total transition-hazard masses are finite and
$A_0\in\mathscr A_{\tau}$.
\item The Nelson--Aalen estimator is row-admissible pathwise:
$\widehat A^{\textsf{AJ}}\in\mathscr A_{\tau}$ for every sample for which the displayed
risk-set ratios are defined with the convention $J_j/\bar Y_j=0$ on
$\{\bar Y_j=0\}$.
\item There are no common calendar-time observed transition jumps in the sample:
\[
J_n^{\max}
    :=\max_{0<u\le\tau}
      \sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal J}\Delta N_{\ell,i}(u)
    \le 1
    \qquad\textnormal{almost surely}.
\]
Consequently $J_n^{\max}=O(1)=o(\sqrt n)$ almost surely.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Assumptions~\ref{ass:time-reg}, \ref{ass:C-ignore}, and~\ref{ass:Markov-state}
imply $\Pr(R_i=T_i)=0$. Thus a subject cannot have simultaneous recurrence and
terminal-event jumps. When both events occur, their times are $R_i$ and
$T_i$ with $R_i<T_i$; when death precedes recurrence, the only observed
transition is $0\to2$. Censoring may remove a transition but cannot create one.

The same assumptions exclude ties between subjects: for $i\ne k$ and
$\ell,r\in\mathcal J$,
$\Pr\{S_{\ell,i}=S_{r,k}<\infty\}=0.$
A finite union over subject and transition pairs gives
$\Pr\{\exists i\ne k,\exists\ell,r,\ S_{\ell,i}=S_{r,k}<\infty\}=0.$
Together with the absence of within-subject simultaneous jumps, this yields
$J_n^{\max}\le1$ almost surely.

For continuity of the compensators, fix $\ell=(j,k)$ and $u\in(0,\tau]$. The absence
of atoms in $S_{\ell,i}$ implies
$\Pr\{\Delta N_{\ell,i}(u)=1\}=0 .$
Taking expectations in the Doob--Meyer decomposition gives
$0=E\{\Delta N_{\ell,i}(u)\} =E\{Y_{j,i}(u)\}\Delta A_{\ell,0}(u) =q_j(u)\Delta A_{\ell,0}(u).$
When $q_j(u)>0$, we obtain $\Delta A_{\ell,0}(u)=0$. When $q_j(u)=0$, the source-support
condition in Assumption~\ref{ass:aj-main-integrated}\ref{ajmain:support}
gives
$\Delta A_{\ell,0}(u) \le \int_0^{\tau}\mathbf 1\{q_j(v)=0\}\,dA_{\ell,0}(v)=0 .$
Hence $A_{\ell,0}$ is continuous. Since $0\le q_j\le1$,
\[
A_{\ell,0}(\tau)
=\int_{(0,\tau]}\mathbf 1\{q_j(u)>0\}\,dA_{\ell,0}(u)
\le
\int_{(0,\tau]}
\frac{\mathbf 1\{q_j(u)>0\}}{q_j(u)}\,dA_{\ell,0}(u)<\infty .
\]
The true hazards therefore have finite mass, and continuity ensures their
row constraints, so $A_0\in\mathscr A_{\tau}$.

Finally, fix a time $u$ and source state $j$. The outgoing
Nelson--Aalen increment from row $j$ is the number of transitions from
subjects at risk in state $j$ just before $u$, divided by the
row-$j$ risk-set size, with value zero for an empty risk set. This
ratio lies in $[0,1]$ because each at-risk subject contributes at most one
outgoing transition. Thus the row constraints defining $\mathscr A_{\tau}$ hold
pathwise for $\widehat A^{\textsf{AJ}}$.

title: Proof
body_md:
The Doob--Meyer decomposition
$d\bar N_\ell(u)=d\bar M_{\ell,0}(u)+\bar Y_j(u)dA_{\ell,0}(u),$
and the convention $J_j/\bar Y_j=0$ on $\bar Y_j=0$ give
$d\{\widehat A_\ell^{\textsf{AJ}}-A_{\ell,0}\}(u) = \frac{J_j(u)}{\bar Y_j(u)}d\bar M_{\ell,0}(u) +\{J_j(u)-1\}dA_{\ell,0}(u).$
Multiplication by $L_\ell=q_jh_\ell$ and addition and subtraction of $\int h_\ell d\bar M_{\ell,0}$ yield
\begin{align*}
\int L_\ell d(\widehat A_\ell^{\textsf{AJ}}-A_{\ell,0})
&=
\int h_\ell d\bar M_{\ell,0}+R_{1,n}+R_{2,n}, \\
R_{1,n}
&=
\int h_\ell(u)
\left\{\frac{q_j(u)J_j(u)}{\bar Y_j(u)}-1\right\}d\bar M_{\ell,0}(u), \\
R_{2,n}
&=
-\int q_j(u)h_\ell(u)\1\{\bar Y_j(u)=0\}dA_{\ell,0}(u).
\end{align*}
For $R_{2,n}$, boundedness $\|h_\ell\|_\infty<\infty$ implies
$E|R_{2,n}| \le \|h_\ell\|_\infty \int_0^{\tau}q_j(u)\Pr\{\bar Y_j(u)=0\}dA_{\ell,0}(u).$
At each fixed $u$, $K_u=n\bar Y_j(u)\sim \mathrm{Binomial}(n,q_j(u))$, and therefore $\Pr\{\bar Y_j(u)=0\}=\{1-q_j(u)\}^n\le e^{-nq_j(u)}$. Since $x e^{-nx}\le(en)^{-1}$,
$E|R_{2,n}| \le \frac{\|h_\ell\|_\infty}{en}A_{\ell,0}(\tau)=O(n^{-1}),$
so $R_{2,n}=O_p(n^{-1})$.

For $R_{1,n}$, the predictable quadratic variation satisfies
\begin{align*}
\langle R_{1,n}\rangle(\tau)
&\le
\frac1{n^2}\sum_{i=1}^n\int_0^{\tau}
 h_\ell(u)^2
\left\{\frac{q_j(u)J_j(u)}{\bar Y_j(u)}-1\right\}^2
Y_{j,i}(u)dA_{\ell,0}(u) \\
&=
\frac1n\int_0^{\tau}
 h_\ell(u)^2
\left\{\frac{q_j(u)J_j(u)}{\bar Y_j(u)}-1\right\}^2
\bar Y_j(u)dA_{\ell,0}(u).
\end{align*}
The integrand vanishes on $\{\bar Y_j(u)=0\}$, whereas on $\{\bar Y_j(u)>0\}$,
$\left\{\frac{q_jJ_j}{\bar Y_j}-1\right\}^2\bar Y_j = \frac{\{q_j-\bar Y_j\}^2}{\bar Y_j}.$
Thus
\begin{equation}
E\langle R_{1,n}\rangle(\tau)
 \le
\frac{\|h_\ell\|_\infty^2}{n}
\int_0^{\tau}
E\left[
\frac{\{q_j(u)-\bar Y_j(u)\}^2}{\bar Y_j(u)}\1\{\bar Y_j(u)>0\}
\right]
dA_{\ell,0}(u).\label{eq:weighted-na-bracket-bound}
\end{equation}
Let $K\sim\mathrm{Binomial}(n,q)$ and $\mu=nq$. Then
$E\left[ \frac{\{q-K/n\}^2}{K/n}\1\{K>0\} \right] = \frac1nE\left[\frac{(K-\mu)^2}{K}\1\{K>0\}\right] \le \frac{C}{n},$
where the last inequality follows by splitting on $\{K\ge \mu/2\}$, applying
Chernoff's bound on $\{K<\mu/2\}$, and handling $\mu<2$ using $(K-\mu)^2K^{-1}\1(K>0)\le2K+2\mu^2\1(K>0)$. Substitution in
\eqref{eq:weighted-na-bracket-bound} gives
$E\langle R_{1,n}\rangle(\tau) \le \frac{C\|h_\ell\|_\infty^2}{n^2}A_{\ell,0}(\tau)=O(n^{-2}).$
Doob's $L_2$ inequality implies $R_{1,n}=O_p(n^{-1})$. Combining this with $R_{2,n}=O_p(n^{-1})$
proves \eqref{eq:weighted-na-linearization}.

body_md:
\label{def:cox-martingale}
For a fixed transition $\ell=(j,k)$, define the subject-level Cox martingale
$M_{\ell,0,i}^{\beta}(t) :=N_{\ell,i}(t) -\int_0^tY_{j,i}(u)e^{\beta_{\ell,0}^\top X_i} d\Lambda_{0,\ell,0}(u)$
at the true parameter.
Its training average is
$\bar M_{\ell,0}^{\beta}(t) :=\mathbb P_{\mathrm{tr},n} M_{\ell,0}^{\beta}(t) =n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^nM_{\ell,0,i}^{\beta}(t),$
and hence, in differential notation,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:cox-average-martingale}
    d\bar M_{\ell,0}^{\beta}(u)
    :=\mathbb P_{\mathrm{tr},n} dN_\ell(u)-S_{\ell,n}^{(0)}(\beta_{\ell,0},u)
      d\Lambda_{0,\ell,0}(u).
\end{equation}
Here $\mathbb P_{\mathrm{tr},n} dN_\ell(u):=n^{-1}\sum_i dN_{\ell,i}(u)$.

\label{lem:cox-no-ties}
Under Assumptions~\ref{ass:time-reg}, \ref{ass:C-ignore}, \ref{ass:Markov-state}, and~\ref{ass:cox-main-primitives}, for each
transition $\ell\in\mathcal J$,
\[
\mathcal T_{\ell,n}:=
\max_{0<u\le\tau}n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\Delta N_{\ell,i}(u)
\le n^{-1}
\qquad\textnormal{almost surely}.

title: Proof
body_md:
The path-level no-ties argument in the proof of
Lemma~\ref{lem:aj-jump-regularity} applies under the same
standing continuity and independent-sampling assumptions, conditionally on
the covariates and then after taking expectations. Censoring can remove
but cannot create a transition jump. Thus at most one subject contributes
a transition-$\ell$ jump at a calendar time, and
$\mathcal T_{\ell,n}\le n^{-1}$ almost surely.

To establish continuity of the baseline hazard, fix $u\in(0,\tau]$. The time
$S_\ell$ has no conditional atom and hence no unconditional atom, giving
$\Pr\{\Delta N_\ell(u)=1\}=0$. The Cox model implies
$E\{\Delta N_\ell(u)\} =E\{Y_j(u)e^{\beta_{\ell,0}^{\top}X}\}\Delta\Lambda_{0,\ell,0}(u) =s_{\ell,0}(u)\Delta\Lambda_{0,\ell,0}(u).$
When $s_{\ell,0}(u)>0$, this gives $\Delta\Lambda_{0,\ell,0}(u)=0$. When $s_{\ell,0}(u)=0$, the source-support
convention \eqref{eq:cox-main-source-support} gives
$\Delta\Lambda_{0,\ell,0}(u) \le \int_{(0,\tau]}\mathbf 1\{s_{\ell,0}(v)=0\} d\Lambda_{0,\ell,0}(v)=0 .$
Thus $\Lambda_{0,\ell,0}$ is continuous. Bounded covariates also imply
$0\le s_{\ell,0}(u) =E\{Y_j(u)e^{\beta_{\ell,0}^{\top}X}\} \le e^{\|\beta_{\ell,0}\|K}=:C_\ell .$
The source-support convention and the finite inverse-risk condition now give
\[
\Lambda_{0,\ell,0}(\tau)
=\int_{(0,\tau]}\mathbf 1\{s_{\ell,0}(u)>0\}
  d\Lambda_{0,\ell,0}(u)
\le
C_\ell
\int_{(0,\tau]}
\frac{\mathbf 1\{s_{\ell,0}(u)>0\}}{s_{\ell,0}(u)}
  d\Lambda_{0,\ell,0}(u)<\infty .
\]
as required.

label: lem:cox-risk-regularity
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:cox-risk-regularity}
Fix a transition $\ell=(j,k)$, and let
$s_\ell^{(r)}(\beta,u)=E\{Y_j(u)e^{\beta^\top X}X^{\otimes r}\}, \qquad r=0,1,2.$
Let $\mathcal B_\ell$ be a bounded neighborhood of $\beta_{\ell,0}$, and set
$R_\ell=\sup_{\beta\in\mathcal B_\ell}\|\beta\|$.    If, in addition,
$P\{Y_j(u_m)\ne Y_j(u)\}\to0$ whenever $u_m\to u$, then the risk functions are
also continuous in $u$ .
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textnormal{(\alph*)}]
\item If $\|X\|\le K$ a.s., then for $r=0,1,2$,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:cox-risk-envelope}
    \sup_{(\beta,u)\in\mathcal B_\ell\times[0,\tau]}
    \|s_\ell^{(r)}(\beta,u)\|
    \le e^{R_\ell K}K^r <\infty,
\end{equation}
and for $r=0,1,2$,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:cox-risk-lipschitz}
    \sup_{u\le\tau}
    \|s_\ell^{(r)}(\beta,u)-s_\ell^{(r)}(\beta',u)\|
    \le e^{R_\ell K}K^{r+1}\|\beta-\beta'\|,
    \qquad \beta,\beta'\in\mathcal B_\ell .
\end{equation}
Moreover, for every fixed $u$, $\beta\mapsto s_\ell^{(r)}(\beta,u)$ is
continuous on $\mathcal B_\ell$.  If the optional at-risk path continuity stated
above holds, then $(\beta,u)\mapsto s_\ell^{(r)}(\beta,u)$ is continuous on
$\mathcal B_\ell\times[0,\tau]$.

\item If instead the Cox dimension is fixed and $X$ is sub-Gaussian, then the same
conclusions hold with deterministic finite constants
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:cox-risk-subgaussian-envelope}
    C_{r,\ell}:=E\{e^{R_\ell\|X\|}\|X\|^r\}<\infty,
    \qquad
    L_{r,\ell}:=E\{e^{R_\ell\|X\|}\|X\|^{r+1}\}<\infty,
\end{equation}
in place of $e^{R_\ell K}K^r$ and $e^{R_\ell K}K^{r+1}$, respectively.
That is,
$
\sup_{(\beta,u)}\|s_\ell^{(r)}(\beta,u)\|\le C_{r,\ell} ,
$
and
$
\sup_u\|s_\ell^{(r)}(\beta,u)-s_\ell^{(r)}(\beta',u)\| \le L_{r,\ell}\|\beta-\beta'\| .
$
The fixed-$u$ $\beta$-continuity conclusion again holds, and the joint
$(\beta,u)$-continuity conclusion holds under the optional at-risk path
continuity stated above.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose first that $\|X\|\le K$. The bounds $0\le Y_j(u)\le1$ and $\|\beta\|\le R_\ell$ on $\mathcal B_\ell$
imply
$\|Y_j(u)e^{\beta^\top X}X^{\otimes r}\| \le e^{R_\ell K}K^r.$
Taking expectations proves \eqref{eq:cox-risk-envelope}.
For $\beta,\beta'\in\mathcal B_\ell$, the mean-value theorem gives
$|e^{\beta^\top X}-e^{\beta'^\top X}| \le e^{R_\ell K}|X^\top(\beta-\beta')| \le e^{R_\ell K}K\|\beta-\beta'\|.$
Multiplication by $Y_j(u)\|X\|^r$, followed by expectation and the bound $\|X\|\le K$,
proves \eqref{eq:cox-risk-lipschitz}.

At fixed $u$, convergence $\beta_m\to\beta$ implies
$Y_j(u)e^{\beta_m^\top X}X^{\otimes r} \to Y_j(u)e^{\beta^\top X}X^{\otimes r}$
almost surely. Moreover, $e^{R_\ell K}K^r$ permits dominated convergence, giving
continuity at fixed $u$ in $\beta$. Under the optional at-risk path
continuity condition, let $(\beta_m,u_m)\to(\beta,u)$. Decomposing the difference into a term
containing $Y_j(u_m)-Y_j(u)$ and a term containing $e^{\beta_m^\top X}-e^{\beta^\top X}$ gives joint continuity
in $(\beta,u)$ by the same argument.

In the sub-Gaussian case, fixed dimension implies a Gaussian tail for
$\|X\|$. For sufficiently small $\eta>0$, we therefore have $E\exp\{\eta\|X\|^2\}<\infty$.
The inequality $R_\ell\|X\|\le \eta\|X\|^2+R_\ell^2/(4\eta)$ implies $E\{e^{R_\ell\|X\|}\|X\|^m\}<\infty$ for every fixed integer $m$,
so the constants in \eqref{eq:cox-risk-subgaussian-envelope} are finite.
The  bounds follow respectively from
$\|Y_j(u)e^{\beta^\top X}X^{\otimes r}\| \le e^{R_\ell\|X\|}\|X\|^r$
and
$|e^{\beta^\top X}-e^{\beta'^\top X}|\, \|X\|^r \le e^{R_\ell\|X\|}\|X\|^{r+1}\|\beta-\beta'\|.$
At fixed $u$, continuity in $\beta$ follows by dominated convergence
with  $e^{R_\ell\|X\|}\|X\|^r$. Under the optional at-risk path continuity condition,
the preceding decomposition also gives joint continuity in $(\beta,u)$:
its first term converges to zero in probability and is uniformly integrable.

label: eq:cox-population-score
title: Proof
body_md:
Write $\beta_0=\beta_{\ell,0}$, $\Lambda_0=\Lambda_{0,\ell,0}$, $s^{(r)}=s_\ell^{(r)}$, $s_0=s_{\ell,0}$, $\bar x=\bar z_\ell$, and $V=V_\ell$.
Correct specification of the Cox model gives
$E\{dN_\ell(u)\mid X,\mathcal F_{u-}\} =Y_j(u)e^{\beta_0^\top X}\,d\Lambda_0(u).$
Fubini's theorem and finiteness of the hazard mass yield
\begin{align}
U_\ell(\beta)
&=E\int_0^{\tau}\{X-\bar x(\beta,u)\}\,dN_\ell(u) \notag \\
&=\int_{(0,\tau]}
   E\big[\{X-\bar x(\beta,u)\}Y_j(u)e^{\beta_0^\top X}\big]
   \,d\Lambda_0(u) \notag \\
&=\int_{(0,\tau]}
   \{s^{(1)}(\beta_0,u)-\bar x(\beta,u)s^{(0)}(\beta_0,u)\}
   \,d\Lambda_0(u).                         \label{eq:cox-population-score}
\end{align}
On $s_0(u)>0$, $\bar x(\beta_0,u)=s^{(1)}(\beta_0,u)/s^{(0)}(\beta_0,u)$; on $s_0(u)=0$, the support convention
\eqref{eq:cox-main-source-support} excludes $d\Lambda_0$-mass.
It follows from \eqref{eq:cox-population-score} that $U_\ell(\beta_0)=0$.

For fixed $u$, differentiation of $\bar x(\beta,u)=s^{(1)}(\beta,u)/s^{(0)}(\beta,u)$ on the source support gives
the risk-set covariance
$\partial_\beta \bar x(\beta,u) =\frac{s^{(2)}(\beta,u)}{s^{(0)}(\beta,u)} -\bar x(\beta,u)^{\otimes2} =V(\beta,u),$
with both sides set to zero off the support. Since $\|X\|\le K$ in the main
Cox theorem, $\|V(\beta,u)\|\le 2K^2$. Dominated convergence therefore justifies
differentiation under the integral in \eqref{eq:cox-population-score},
proving \eqref{eq:cox-population-score-derivative}. Evaluation at $\beta_0$ gives
$-\dot U_\ell(\beta_0) =\int_{(0,\tau]}V(\beta_0,u)s_0(u)\,d\Lambda_0(u) =I_\ell,$
as required.

For local invertibility, Lemma~\ref{lem:cox-risk-regularity} gives
boundedness and continuity at fixed $u$ in $\beta$ of $s^{(r)}(\beta,u)$ for
$r=0,1,2$. On $s_0(u)>0$, the map
$V(\beta,u) =\frac{s^{(2)}(\beta,u)}{s^{(0)}(\beta,u)} -\bar x(\beta,u)^{\otimes2}$
is continuous in $\beta$ at fixed $u$. Off this support, the
integrand in \eqref{eq:cox-population-score-derivative} is zero, and
\eqref{eq:cox-main-source-support} excludes $d\Lambda_0$-mass.
The bound $\|X\|\le K$ implies $\|V(\beta,u)\|\le2K^2$ uniformly in $(\beta,u)$.
For $\beta_m\to\beta_0$, dominated convergence thus gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\|\dot U_\ell(\beta_m)-\dot U_\ell(\beta_0)\|
&\le
\int_{(0,\tau]}
\|V(\beta_m,u)-V(\beta_0,u)\|s_0(u)\,d\Lambda_0(u)\\
&\longrightarrow0,
\end{aligned}
\]
because $s_0(u)\le E e^{\beta_0^\top X}\le e^{\|\beta_0\|K}$ and $\Lambda_0(\tau)<\infty$. There is consequently $\delta_\ell>0$ such that
$\sup_{\|\beta-\beta_0\|\le\delta_\ell} \|\dot U_\ell(\beta)-\dot U_\ell(\beta_0)\| \le \iota_\ell/4 .$
Intersecting the original neighborhood with $\mathcal B_\ell\cap\{\beta:\|\beta-\beta_0\|<\delta_\ell\}$ and, if necessary,
taking a smaller open convex ball about $\beta_0$ proves
\eqref{eq:cox-local-information-bound}. The required local invertibility
therefore follows from continuity of the population derivative and the
information lower bound.

label: lem:cox-denominator-bounds
title: Lemma
head: environment

label: eq:cox-risk-count-comparison
title: Proof
body_md:
Let $K_n(u)=\sum_iY_{j,i}(u)$ and $q(u)=P\{Y_j(u)=1\}$.
Bounded covariates and coefficients give constants $0<c<C<\infty$,
depending only on $(K,R)$, such that
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:cox-risk-count-comparison}
cK_n(u)/n\le S_n(u)\le CK_n(u)/n,
\qquad cq(u)\le s(u)\le Cq(u).
\end{equation}
Hence $J_n=\mathbf1\{K_n>0\}$ and $K_n\sim\mathrm{Binomial}(n,q)$.
The case $q=0$ is immediate under the zero-denominator convention.
For $q>0$, $q(1-q)^n\le(en)^{-1}$ proves
\eqref{eq:cox-denominator-zero}.

Suppress $u$ and use the three regimes
$A_1=\{K_n\ge nq/2\}$,
$A_2=\{0<K_n<nq/2,\ nq\ge2\}$, and
$A_3=\{K_n>0,\ nq<2\}$.
The last regime is used when $nq<2$, and the first two when $nq\ge2$.
On $A_1$, \eqref{eq:cox-risk-count-comparison} and
$E(S_n-s)^2\le Cq/n$ give
\[
E\left\{\frac{(S_n-s)^2}{S_n}\mathbf1_{A_1}\right\}
+E\left\{s\frac{(S_n-s)^2}{S_n^2}\mathbf1_{A_1}\right\}
\le Cn^{-1}.
\]
On $A_2$, the two integrands are at most $Cnq^2$ and $Cn^2q^3$,
respectively, while Chernoff's inequality gives $P(A_2)\le e^{-cnq}$.
Their expectations are therefore at most
$Cn^{-1}(nq)^2e^{-cnq}$ and $Cn^{-1}(nq)^3e^{-cnq}$, both bounded by
$Cn^{-1}$. On $A_3$, the elementary inequalities
$(a-b)^2/a\le2a+2b^2/a$ and $(a-b)^2/a^2\le2+2b^2/a^2$
give, respectively,
$\frac{(S_n-s)^2}{S_n}\le C\{K_n/n+nq^2\}$, $s\frac{(S_n-s)^2}{S_n^2}\le C\{q+n^2q^3\}\le Cq$.
Taking expectations and using $nq<2$ bounds both contributions by $Cn^{-1}$.
The first integrand is zero when $S_n=0$; the second ratio expression in
\eqref{eq:cox-denominator-weighted-ratio} then contributes
$sP(S_n=0)\le Cn^{-1}$. This proves
\eqref{eq:cox-denominator-ratio} and \eqref{eq:cox-denominator-weighted-ratio}.

The inverse and higher moments use the same regimes. For a fixed integer
$m\ge1$, on $A_1$ the ratio $nq/K_n$ is at most two. On $A_2$, its
$m$th moment is at most $(nq)^me^{-cnq}$, up to a fixed constant.
On $A_3$, $nq/K_n<2$. Consequently,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:binomial-ratio-moments}
E\left\{(nq/K_n)^m\mathbf1(K_n>0)\right\}\le C_m,
\qquad
E\left\{\frac{q^m\mathbf1(K_n>0)}{(K_n/n)^{m-1}}\right\}\le C_mq.
\end{equation}
For the second inequality, use
$q^m/(K_n/n)^{m-1}=q(nq/K_n)^{m-1}$ on $K_n>0$;
the same reasoning also gives
$E\{q^m\mathbf1(K_n>0)/(K_n/n)^m\}\le C_m\mathbf1(q>0)$.
Transferring these bounds through \eqref{eq:cox-risk-count-comparison} proves
\eqref{eq:cox-denominator-moment-ratio}--\eqref{eq:cox-denominator-moment-inverse}.
The case $m=1$ yields \eqref{eq:cox-denominator-inverse}; division by
$s$ on its positive support yields \eqref{eq:cox-denominator-inverse-risk}.

label: lem:cox-self-normalized-ratios
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:cox-self-normalized-ratios}
Fix a transition $\ell=(j,k)$.  Work under Assumption~\ref{ass:cox-main-primitives}.
Let $\mathcal B_\ell$ be a fixed compact neighborhood of $\beta_{\ell,0}$.
Let $g_\beta(u,x)$ be a scalar or fixed-dimensional vector family satisfying
$\sup_{\beta,u,x}\|g_\beta(u,x)\|\le C_g$, $\sup_{u,x}\|g_\beta(u,x)-g_{\beta'}(u,x)\| \le L_g\|\beta-\beta'\|$,
and assume the corresponding class is bounded Euclidean.  Define
$G_n(\beta,u)=\mathbb P_{\mathrm{tr},n}\{Y_j(u)e^{\beta^\top X}g_\beta(u,X)\}$, $G(\beta,u)=P\{Y_j(u)e^{\beta^\top X}g_\beta(u,X)\}$,
$\bar g_n(\beta,u)= \frac{J_{\ell,n}(u)G_n(\beta,u)}{S_{\ell,n}^{(0)}(\beta,u)}$, $\bar g(\beta,u)= \frac{\mathbf 1\{s_\ell^{(0)}(\beta,u)>0\}G(\beta,u)} {s_\ell^{(0)}(\beta,u)}$,
with ratios equal to zero when their denominators are zero.  Then, for every fixed
$\beta\in\mathcal B_\ell$,
\begin{align}
\label{eq:selfnorm-compensator-rate}
\int_0^{\tau}
\|\bar g_n(\beta,u)-\bar g(\beta,u)\|
S_{\ell,n}^{(0)}(\beta_{\ell,0},u)d\Lambda_{0,\ell,0}(u)
&=O_p(n^{-1/2}), \\
\label{eq:selfnorm-counting-rate}
\mathbb P_{\mathrm{tr},n}\int_0^{\tau}
\|\bar g_n(\beta,u)-\bar g(\beta,u)\|dN_\ell(u)
&=O_p(n^{-1/2}).
\end{align}
Moreover, the corresponding suprema over $\beta\in\mathcal B_\ell$ are
$o_p(1)$.  In particular, the fixed-$\beta$ statement applies at
$\beta=\beta_{\ell,0}$, and the uniform $o_p(1)$ statement applies with
$g_\beta(u,x)=z_r$ and with $g_\beta(u,x)=z_rz_s$.
head: environment

label: eq:selfnorm-denominator-comparison
title: Proof
body_md:
Write $\beta_0=\beta_{\ell,0}$, $S_n(\beta,u)=S_{\ell,n}^{(0)}(\beta,u)$, $s(\beta,u)=s_\ell^{(0)}(\beta,u)$, $s_0(u)=s(\beta_0,u)$, $J=J_{\ell,n}$, and $d\Lambda_0=d\Lambda_{0,\ell,0}$.
Constants may depend on the fixed compact set $\mathcal B_\ell$, but not on
$n,u$ or $\beta$. Bounded covariates give
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:selfnorm-denominator-comparison}
    cS_n(\beta_0,u)\le S_n(\beta,u)\le CS_n(\beta_0,u),
    \qquad
    cs_0(u)\le s(\beta,u)\le Cs_0(u) .
\end{equation}
and $\|G(\beta,u)\|\le C s(\beta,u)$ by boundedness of $g_\beta$.

The denominator estimates needed below hold uniformly in $\beta\in\mathcal B_\ell$:
\begin{align}
\label{eq:selfnorm-ratio-square-bound}
E\left[
S_n(\beta_0,u)
\left\{\frac{s(\beta,u)J(u)}{S_n(\beta,u)}
      -\mathbf 1\{s(\beta,u)>0\}\right\}^{2}
\right]&\le C n^{-1}, \\
\label{eq:selfnorm-ratio-l1-bound}
E\left[
S_n(\beta_0,u)
\left|\frac{s(\beta,u)J(u)}{S_n(\beta,u)}
      -\mathbf 1\{s(\beta,u)>0\}\right|
\right]&\le C n^{-1/2}s_0(u)^{1/2}.
\end{align}
The first follows from \eqref{eq:cox-denominator-ratio}, transferred
from $\beta_0$ to $\beta$ through \eqref{eq:selfnorm-denominator-comparison}.
For the second, Cauchy--Schwarz
with $R_n=s(\beta,u)J/S_n(\beta,u)-\mathbf 1\{s(\beta,u)>0\}$,
gives
$E\{S_n|R_n|\} \le \{ES_n\}^{1/2}\{E(S_nR_n^2)\}^{1/2} \le C s_0(u)^{1/2}n^{-1/2}$.

For fixed $\beta$, decompose
$\bar g_n(\beta,u)-\bar g(\beta,u)=A_n(\beta,u)+B_n(\beta,u),$
with
$A_n(\beta,u)=\frac{J}{S_n(\beta,u)}\{G_n(\beta,u)-G(\beta,u)\}$
and
$B_n(\beta,u)=G(\beta,u) \left\{ \frac{J}{S_n(\beta,u)}- \frac{\mathbf 1\{s(\beta,u)>0\}}{s(\beta,u)} \right\}.$
At fixed $\beta$, the bounded Euclidean maximal inequality yields
$\Delta_{G,n}(\beta):= \sup_{u\le\tau}\|G_n(\beta,u)-G(\beta,u)\|=O_p(n^{-1/2}).$
We first bound the compensator integral at fixed $\beta$. For $A_n$,
\eqref{eq:selfnorm-denominator-comparison} gives
\[
\int\|A_n(\beta,u)\|S_n(\beta_0,u)d\Lambda_0(u)
\le C\Delta_{G,n}(\beta)\int_0^{\tau}J(u)d\Lambda_0(u)
=O_p(n^{-1/2}),
\]
Here $\Lambda_0(\tau)<\infty$ follows from CX2 and bounded covariates: $s_0(u)\le C$ and
$\Lambda_0(\tau)\le C\int \mathbf 1\{s_0(u)>0\}s_0(u)^{-1}\,d\Lambda_0(u)<\infty$. For $B_n$, use $\|G(\beta,u)\|\le Cs(\beta,u)$ and
\eqref{eq:selfnorm-denominator-comparison} to obtain
\[
\|B_n(\beta,u)\|S_n(\beta_0,u)
\le C S_n(\beta_0,u)
\left|\frac{s(\beta,u)J(u)}{S_n(\beta,u)}
      -\mathbf 1\{s(\beta,u)>0\}\right| .
\]
Taking expectations and applying \eqref{eq:selfnorm-ratio-l1-bound}, with
$s_0\le C$ and $\Lambda_0(\tau)<\infty$, gives
\[
E\int\|B_n(\beta,u)\|S_n(\beta_0,u)d\Lambda_0(u)
\le Cn^{-1/2}\int s_0(u)^{1/2}d\Lambda_0(u)=O(n^{-1/2}).
\]
This proves \eqref{eq:selfnorm-compensator-rate}.

For the counting integral at fixed $\beta$, the decomposition
$\mathbb P_{\mathrm{tr},n} dN_\ell(u)=S_n(\beta_0,u)d\Lambda_0(u)+d\bar M_{\ell,0}^{\beta}(u),$
reduces the remaining argument to the martingale integral with integrand
$f_n(\beta,u)=\|\bar g_n(\beta,u)-\bar g(\beta,u)\|$. The predictable quadratic variation of $\int f_n(\beta,u)d\bar M_{\ell,0}^{\beta}(u)$ is at most
\[
\frac1n\int f_n(\beta,u)^2S_n(\beta_0,u)d\Lambda_0(u).
\]
For $A_n$, this bound is at most
$\frac{C\Delta_{G,n}(\beta)^2}{n} \int_0^{\tau}\frac{J(u)}{S_n(\beta_0,u)}d\Lambda_0(u)=O_p(n^{-2})$,
by \eqref{eq:cox-main-source-support} and
\eqref{eq:cox-denominator-inverse-risk}. For $B_n$,
\eqref{eq:selfnorm-ratio-square-bound} gives
$E\left[\frac1n\int\|B_n(\beta,u)\|^2S_n(\beta_0,u)d\Lambda_0(u)\right] \le Cn^{-2}\Lambda_0(\tau).$
Lenglart's inequality bounds the martingale contribution by $O_p(n^{-1})$.
Together with the compensator bound, this proves
\eqref{eq:selfnorm-counting-rate}.

To obtain the uniform $o_p(1)$ conclusion, we establish stochastic
equicontinuity of the self-normalized component. Differentiating the ratio
and using bounded covariates gives, for $\beta,\beta'\in\mathcal B_\ell$,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:selfnorm-ratio-lipschitz}
\left|\frac{s(\beta,u)J}{S_n(\beta,u)}-
      \frac{s(\beta',u)J}{S_n(\beta',u)}\right|
\le Q_n(u)\|\beta-\beta'\|,
\end{equation}
where
$Q_n(u)=C\left\{1+\frac{Js_0(u)}{S_n(\beta_0,u)} +\frac{Js_0(u)^2}{S_n(\beta_0,u)^2}\right\}.$
With a larger constant and the Euclidean modulus for $g_\beta$, the same
bound controls each scalar coordinate of $\{\bar g_n(\beta,u)-\bar g(\beta,u)\}-
  \{\bar g_n(\beta',u)-\bar g(\beta',u)\}$, apart from the ordinary
empirical-process increment already considered. The moment estimates
\eqref{eq:cox-denominator-moment-ratio}--\eqref{eq:cox-denominator-moment-inverse}
imply, for every fixed integer $r\ge1$,
\begin{align}
\label{eq:selfnorm-envelope-moment}
E\left[\left\{
\int_0^{\tau}Q_n(u)^2S_n(\beta_0,u)d\Lambda_0(u)
\right\}^r\right]&\le C_r, \\
\label{eq:selfnorm-jump-envelope-moment}
E\int_0^{\tau}Q_n(u)^{2r}S_n(\beta_0,u)d\Lambda_0(u)&\le C_r.
\end{align}
Indeed, expanding the powers of $Q_n$ gives expectations of $s_0(u)^mJ/S_n(\beta_0,u)^{m-1}$
and expectations of $s_0(u)^mJ/S_n(\beta_0,u)^m$, controlled by \eqref{eq:cox-denominator-moment-weighted} and
\eqref{eq:cox-denominator-moment-inverse}.
The remaining integrals are finite because $s_0(u)\le C$ and $\Lambda_0(\tau)<\infty$, by CX2 and bounded covariates.

For the compensator term, \eqref{eq:selfnorm-ratio-lipschitz} and
\eqref{eq:selfnorm-envelope-moment}, together with the ordinary Euclidean
empirical-process modulus, give
\[
\sup_{\beta\ne\beta'}
\frac{
\int \|D_n(\beta,u)-D_n(\beta',u)\|S_n(\beta_0,u)d\Lambda_0(u)}
{\|\beta-\beta'\|}
=O_p(1),
\]
where $D_n(\beta,u)=\bar g_n(\beta,u)-\bar g(\beta,u)$. A fixed $\varepsilon$-net, followed by $n\to\infty$ and then
$\varepsilon\downarrow0$, therefore bounds the compensator supremum by $o_p(1)$.

For a scalar coordinate of the martingale term, put
$M_n(\beta)=\int_0^{\tau}D_n(\beta,u)d\bar M_{\ell,0}^{\beta}(u)$, $\Delta_n(\beta,\beta')=M_n(\beta)-M_n(\beta')$.
For any integer $r>p_\ell+2$, the purely discontinuous Burkholder--Davis--Gundy
inequality\citep{jacod1975multivariate}, the bracket bound, \eqref{eq:selfnorm-ratio-lipschitz}, and
\eqref{eq:selfnorm-envelope-moment} give
\begin{align}
\label{eq:selfnorm-martingale-increment}
E|\Delta_n(\beta,\beta')|^{2r}
&\le
C_r E\{\langle\Delta_n(\beta,\beta')\rangle(\tau)^r\}
+C_rE\sum_{u\le\tau}|\Delta\Delta_n(\beta,\beta';u)|^{2r} \\
&\le C_r n^{-r}\|\beta-\beta'\|^{2r}. \notag
\end{align}
For the jump contribution, Lemma~\ref{lem:cox-no-ties} implies
$\Delta\bar M_{\ell,0}^{\beta}(u)=\Delta\mathbb P_{\mathrm{tr},n} N_\ell(u)\le n^{-1}$. Hence
\[
E\sum_{u\le\tau}|\Delta\Delta_n(\beta,\beta';u)|^{2r}
\le
C_r n^{-2r+1}\|\beta-\beta'\|^{2r}
E\int Q_n(u)^{2r}S_n(\beta_0,u)d\Lambda_0(u),
\]
which is bounded by the right-hand side of
\eqref{eq:selfnorm-martingale-increment}, since $r\ge1$ and
\eqref{eq:selfnorm-jump-envelope-moment} holds.

Let $T_m$ be a Euclidean $2^{-m}$-net of $\mathcal B_\ell$ with $|T_m|\le C2^{mp_\ell}$.
Chaining from a fixed coarse net and applying Markov's inequality with
\eqref{eq:selfnorm-martingale-increment} gives, for $A>0$,
\[
\Pr\left(
\max_{\text{level }m\text{ pairs}}
|M_n(t)-M_n(s)|>A n^{-1/2}2^{-m/2}
\right)
\le C_rA^{-2r}2^{-m(r-p_\ell)} .
\]
Because $r>p_\ell+2$, the bound is summable in $m$. The finitely many
coarse-net values converge to zero by the fixed-$\beta$ martingale bound,
and the chained increments are $O_p(n^{-1/2})$. Thus
$\sup_{\beta\in\mathcal B_\ell}|M_n(\beta)|=o_p(1).$
Combining martingale and compensator equicontinuity shows that the
counting-integral supremum over $\mathcal B_\ell$ is $o_p(1)$.

label: lem:cox-empirical-score
title: Lemma
head: environment

label: eq:cox-counting-empirical-process
title: Proof
body_md:
Fixed dimension allows us to work coordinatewise and take finite maxima.
Suppress the transition subscript and write $\beta_0=\beta_{\ell,0}$, $\Lambda_0=\Lambda_{0,\ell,0}$, $S_n^{(r)}=S_{\ell,n}^{(r)}$,
$s^{(r)}=s_\ell^{(r)}$, $\bar Z_n=\bar Z_{\ell,n}$, and $\bar x=\bar z_\ell$. For $r=0,1,2,3$, the class
$\mathcal F_r= \{O\mapsto Y_j(u)e^{\beta^\top X}X^{\otimes r}: \beta\in\mathcal B_\ell, 0\le u\le\tau\}$
is bounded and Euclidean, so
$\sup_{\beta\in\mathcal B_\ell,\,u\le\tau} \|S_n^{(r)}(\beta,u)-s^{(r)}(\beta,u)\|=O_p(n^{-1/2})$, $r=0,1,2,3$.
Likewise, for a bounded, fixed-dimensional Lipschitz family $g_\beta(u,x)$,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:cox-counting-empirical-process}
    \sup_{\beta\in\mathcal B_\ell}
    \left|
    (\mathbb P_{\mathrm{tr},n}-P)\int_0^{\tau}g_\beta(u,X)dN_\ell(u)
    \right|=O_p(n^{-1/2}).
\end{equation}
This applies to $g_{\beta_0}(u,X)=X-\bar x(\beta_0,u)$ and to each scalar entry of $V(\beta,u)$, since
$\bar x$ and $V$ are bounded and locally Lipschitz by
Lemma~\ref{lem:cox-risk-regularity}.

At $\beta_0$, adding and subtracting the population risk-set mean gives
\begin{align*}
U_n(\beta_0)-U(\beta_0)
&=(\mathbb P_{\mathrm{tr},n}-P)\int_0^{\tau}\{X-\bar x(\beta_0,u)\}dN_\ell(u) \\
&\quad+
\mathbb P_{\mathrm{tr},n}\int_0^{\tau}\{\bar x(\beta_0,u)-\bar Z_n(\beta_0,u)\}dN_\ell(u).
\end{align*}
The first term is $O_p(n^{-1/2})$ by \eqref{eq:cox-counting-empirical-process}.
The second is $O_p(n^{-1/2})$ by the fixed-$\beta$ conclusion of
Lemma~\ref{lem:cox-self-normalized-ratios}, with $g_\beta(u,x)=x$ at
$\beta=\beta_0$. Since $U(\beta_0)=0$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:cox-population-score}, this
proves \eqref{eq:cox-score-at-truth}.

The derivative difference has the decomposition
\[
\dot U_n(\beta)-\dot U(\beta)
=-(\mathbb P_{\mathrm{tr},n}-P)\int_0^{\tau}V(\beta,u)dN_\ell(u)
-
\mathbb P_{\mathrm{tr},n}\int_0^{\tau}\{V_n(\beta,u)-V(\beta,u)\}dN_\ell(u).
\]
The first term is uniformly $O_p(n^{-1/2})$ by
\eqref{eq:cox-counting-empirical-process}. For the second, write
\[
V_n-V=
\left\{\frac{J_nS_n^{(2)}}{S_n^{(0)}}-
       \frac{j_0s^{(2)}}{s^{(0)}}\right\}
-
\left\{\bar Z_n^{\otimes2}-\bar x^{\otimes2}\right\}.
\]
Each entry of the first bracket is a self-normalized ratio error covered
by Lemma~\ref{lem:cox-self-normalized-ratios} with $g_\beta(u,x)=z_rz_s$.
Its integral against $\mathbb P_{\mathrm{tr},n} dN_\ell$ is therefore uniformly over $\beta\in\mathcal B_\ell$ of
order $o_p(1)$. For the second bracket,
$\|\bar Z_n^{\otimes2}-\bar x^{\otimes2}\| \le \|\bar Z_n-\bar x\|\{\|\bar Z_n\|+\|\bar x\|\} \le 2K\|\bar Z_n-\bar x\|$,
The same lemma with $g_\beta(u,x)=x$ gives a uniformly $o_p(1)$ integral.
Consequently, $\mathcal D_{\ell,n}=o_p(1)$, proving \eqref{eq:cox-score-derivative-uniform}.

label: eq:cox-local-curvature
title: Proof
body_md:
The criterion $Q_{\ell,n}=-\ell_{\ell,n}$ is continuous and convex on the
compact convex set $\Theta_\ell$, so its minimizer set is nonempty.
Since $\beta_{\ell,0}$ is interior, a fixed neighborhood of it lies inside
$\Theta_\ell$. On that neighborhood,
Lemmas~\ref{lem:cox-population-score} and
\ref{lem:cox-empirical-score} give local curvature and
uniform convergence of the score derivative. More precisely, for any
$\eta>0$, choose $L<\infty$ so that, for all sufficiently large $n$, the event
$\mathcal E_n(L)=\{\sqrt n\|U_{\ell,n}(\beta_{\ell,0})\|\le L, \ \mathcal D_{\ell,n}\le\iota_\ell/4\}$
has probability at least $1-\eta$.
For fixed $M$, the ball
$B_n(M)=\{\beta:\|\beta-\beta_{\ell,0}\|\le Mn^{-1/2}\}$ lies inside
that neighborhood for large $n$. The population derivative differs from
$\dot U_\ell(\beta_{\ell,0})=-I_\ell$ by at most $\iota_\ell/4$ there.
Since $\lambda_{\min}(I_\ell)\ge\iota_\ell$, on $\mathcal E_n(L)$,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:cox-local-curvature}
v^\top\dot U_{\ell,n}(\beta)v
\le-\frac{\iota_\ell}{2}\|v\|^2,
\qquad \beta\in B_n(M).
\end{equation}
For $\|h\|=M$, Taylor's formula and
\eqref{eq:cox-local-curvature} imply
\[
\ell_{\ell,n}(\beta_{\ell,0}+n^{-1/2}h)
 -\ell_{\ell,n}(\beta_{\ell,0})
\le n^{-1}\{LM-\iota_\ell M^2/4\}<0
\]
when $M>4L/\iota_\ell$. Thus the maximizer over $B_n(M)$ is interior;
strict concavity there makes it unique and gives the score equation.
It is also the global maximizer over $\Theta_\ell$: an exterior point
with at least as large a criterion value would, by concavity along the
joining segment, give a boundary point with criterion value at least
$\ell_{\ell,n}(\beta_{\ell,0})$, contradicting the displayed inequality.
Consequently the estimator in \eqref{eq:cox-beta-hat-def} is this unique
interior maximizer on $\mathcal E_n(L)$ and satisfies
$\|\widehat\beta_\ell-\beta_{\ell,0}\|\le Mn^{-1/2}$ and
$U_{\ell,n}(\widehat\beta_\ell)=0$.
Since $\eta$ was arbitrary, the asserted rate, interiority, and uniqueness follow.

label: lem:breslow-rates

head: environment

label: eq:breslow-truth-decomposition
title: Proof
body_md:
Write $\beta_0=\beta_{\ell,0}$, $\widehat\beta=\widehat\beta_\ell$, $S_n(\beta,u)=S_{\ell,n}^{(0)}(\beta,u)$, and $s_0(u)=s_{\ell,0}(u)$. We first control the
Breslow estimator at $\beta_0$, then the effect of replacing $\beta_0$ by
$\widehat\beta$, and finally its squared jumps. Define
$\widetilde\Lambda_{0,\ell}(t)=\int_0^t\frac{J_{\ell,n}(u)}{S_n(\beta_0,u)}\,\mathbb P_{\mathrm{tr},n} dN_\ell(u).$
The training-average martingale decomposition in
Definition~\ref{def:cox-martingale} gives
$\mathbb P_{\mathrm{tr},n} dN_\ell(u)=d\bar M_{\ell,0}^{\beta}(u)+S_n(\beta_0,u)d\Lambda_{0,\ell,0}(u)$.
and therefore
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:breslow-truth-decomposition}
\widetilde\Lambda_{0,\ell}(t)-\Lambda_{0,\ell,0}(t)
 =
\int_0^t\frac{J_{\ell,n}(u)}{S_n(\beta_0,u)}\,d\bar M_{\ell,0}^{\beta}(u)
-
\int_0^t\mathbf 1\{S_n(\beta_0,u)=0\}\,d\Lambda_{0,\ell,0}(u).
\end{equation}

Since $S_n(\beta_0,u)=0$ is equivalent to an empty empirical source-state risk set,
\eqref{eq:cox-denominator-zero} in
Lemma~\ref{lem:cox-denominator-bounds} gives
$P\{S_n(\beta_0,u)=0\} \le C n^{-1}\frac{\mathbf 1\{s_0(u)>0\}}{s_0(u)}$
for $d\Lambda_{0,\ell,0}$-almost every $u$. The set $\{s_0=0\}$ has no baseline-hazard
mass by \eqref{eq:cox-main-source-support}. Hence
$E\int_0^{\tau}\mathbf 1\{S_n(\beta_0,u)=0\}\,d\Lambda_{0,\ell,0}(u) \le Cn^{-1}V_\ell^{\mathrm{cox}}=O(n^{-1}).$
Thus the zero-risk term in \eqref{eq:breslow-truth-decomposition} is $O_p(n^{-1})$
uniformly in $t$. The martingale term has predictable quadratic
variation bounded by
$\frac1n\int_0^t\frac{J_{\ell,n}(u)}{S_n(\beta_0,u)}\,d\Lambda_{0,\ell,0}(u)$.
Taking expectations and using \eqref{eq:cox-denominator-inverse-risk} gives
\[
E\left\langle\int_0^\cdot\frac{J_{\ell,n}}{S_n(\beta_0)}d\bar M_{\ell,0}^{\beta}\right\rangle(\tau)
\le \frac{C}{n}\int\frac{\mathbf 1\{s_0(u)>0\}}{s_0(u)}d\Lambda_{0,\ell,0}(u)
=O(n^{-1}).
\]
Doob's $L_2$ inequality yields
$\sup_{t\le\tau}\left|\int_0^t\frac{J_{\ell,n}}{S_n(\beta_0)}d\bar M_{\ell,0}^{\beta}\right| =O_p(n^{-1/2}).$
Combining the two bounds, we obtain
$\sup_{t\le\tau}|\widetilde\Lambda_{0,\ell}(t)-\Lambda_{0,\ell,0}(t)| =O_p(n^{-1/2})$, $\widetilde\Lambda_{0,\ell}(\tau)=O_p(1)$.
To replace $\beta_0$ by $\widehat\beta$, work on $\|\widehat\beta-\beta_0\|\le1$. Bounded covariates give
$e^{-K\|\widehat\beta-\beta_0\|}S_n(\beta_0,u) \le S_n(\widehat\beta,u) \le e^{K\|\widehat\beta-\beta_0\|}S_n(\beta_0,u).$
Thus, on $J_{\ell,n}=1$,
$\left|\frac{1}{S_n(\widehat\beta,u)}- \frac{1}{S_n(\beta_0,u)}\right| \le C\|\widehat\beta-\beta_0\|\frac{1}{S_n(\beta_0,u)}.$
Consequently,
$\sup_t|\widehat\Lambda_{0,\ell}(t)-\widetilde\Lambda_{0,\ell}(t)| \le C\|\widehat\beta-\beta_0\|\widetilde\Lambda_{0,\ell}(\tau) =O_p(n^{-1/2}),$
by Lemma~\ref{lem:cox-root-consistency}. This proves
\eqref{eq:breslow-sup-rate}.

For the squared jumps, Lemma~\ref{lem:cox-no-ties} ensures that
at most one subject has a transition-$\ell$ jump at any calendar time.
Thus, as discrete measures,
$(\mathbb P_{\mathrm{tr},n} dN_\ell)^2=n^{-1}\mathbb P_{\mathrm{tr},n} dN_\ell.$
On $\|\widehat\beta-\beta_0\|\le1$, the preceding denominator comparison gives
\[
\sum_u\{\Delta\widehat\Lambda_{0,\ell}(u)\}^2
\le
\frac{C}{n}\int_0^{\tau}
\frac{J_{\ell,n}(u)}{S_n(\beta_0,u)^2}\,\mathbb P_{\mathrm{tr},n} dN_\ell(u).
\]
The integrand at $\beta_0$ is predictable, with compensator
$\frac{C}{n}\int_0^{\tau} \frac{J_{\ell,n}(u)}{S_n(\beta_0,u)}\,d\Lambda_{0,\ell,0}(u),$
whose expectation is at most $Cn^{-1}V_\ell^{\mathrm{cox}}$ by
\eqref{eq:cox-denominator-inverse-risk}. Markov's inequality proves
\eqref{eq:breslow-squared-jumps}.

label: eq:cox-risk-mean-decomposition
title: Proof
body_md:
It suffices to work coordinatewise, since the Cox dimension is fixed. Write
$S_n^{(0)}(u)=S_{\ell,n}^{(0)}(\beta_0,u),\qquad S_n^{(1)}(u)=n^{-1}\sum_iY_{j,i}(u)e^{\beta_0^\top X_i}Z_{ir},$
and $s^{(0)}(u)=s_0(u)$, $s^{(1)}(u)=E\{Y_j(u)e^{\beta_0^\top X}Z_r\}$. Put $J(u)=\mathbf 1\{S_n^{(0)}(u)>0\}$. The bound $|Z_r|\le K$ implies $|s^{(1)}(u)|\le K s_0(u)$,
and $s^{(1)}(u)=0$ whenever $s_0(u)=0$. The exact decomposition is
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:cox-risk-mean-decomposition}
s_0J\bar Z_{\ell,n,r}-s_0\bar z_{\ell,r}
 =\frac{s_0J}{S_n^{(0)}}\{S_n^{(1)}-s^{(1)}\}
+s^{(1)}\left\{\frac{s_0J}{S_n^{(0)}}-1\right\}
-s^{(1)}\mathbf 1\{s_0=0\} .
\end{equation}
The last term has zero $d\Lambda_{0,\ell,0}$-mass by
\eqref{eq:cox-main-source-support}.

For the first term, set
$A_n(u)=\frac{s_0(u)J(u)}{S_n^{(0)}(u)}\{S_n^{(1)}(u)-s^{(1)}(u)\}.$
We establish
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:cox-risk-mean-first-moment}
E\{A_n(u)^2\}\le C n^{-1}s_0(u).
\end{equation}
Let $K_n(u)=\sum_iY_{j,i}(u)$ and $q(u)=P\{Y_j(u)=1\}$. As in
Lemma~\ref{lem:cox-denominator-bounds}, $S_n^{(0)}$ and $s_0$ are
comparable to $K_n/n$ and $q$, respectively. Consider $A_1=\{K_n\ge nq/2\}$,
$A_2=\{0<K_n<nq/2,nq\ge2\}$, and $A_3=\{0<K_n,nq<2\}$. On $A_1$, the multiplier $s_0J/S_n^{(0)}$ is bounded,
and
$E\{(S_n^{(1)}-s^{(1)})^2\}\le Cq/n\le C s_0/n,$
so the contribution of $A_1$ is bounded by $Cs_0/n$. On $A_2$,
the multiplier is at most $C nq$ and $|S_n^{(1)}-s^{(1)}|\le C(K_n/n+q)\le Cq$. The integrand is therefore
bounded by $C(nq)^2q^2$, giving contribution $C(nq)^2q^2e^{-cnq}\le Cs_0/n$ by Chernoff's inequality.
On $A_3$, we have $nq<2$ and $s_0J/S_n^{(0)}\le Cnq\le C$, while
$E\{(K_n/n+q)^2\mathbf 1(K_n>0)\}\le Cq/n.$
Thus the contribution of $A_3$ is also bounded by $Cs_0/n$, proving
\eqref{eq:cox-risk-mean-first-moment}.

For the second term in \eqref{eq:cox-risk-mean-decomposition}, use $|s^{(1)}|\le Ks_0$ and
\eqref{eq:cox-denominator-weighted-ratio}. Since $0\le s_0(u)\le C$,
\begin{align}
\label{eq:cox-risk-mean-second-moment}
&E\left[
|s^{(1)}(u)|^2\left\{\frac{s_0(u)J(u)}{S_n^{(0)}(u)}-1\right\}^2
\right] \\
&\qquad\le C s_0(u)
E\left[
s_0(u)\left\{\frac{s_0(u)J(u)}{S_n^{(0)}(u)}-1\right\}^2
\right]
\le C n^{-1}s_0(u). \notag
\end{align}
Let $D_n(u)$ be the sum of the first two terms in
\eqref{eq:cox-risk-mean-decomposition}. Cauchy--Schwarz for the finite measure $d\Lambda_{0,\ell,0}$
gives
\[
E\left[\left\{\int_0^{\tau}h(u)D_n(u)d\Lambda_{0,\ell,0}(u)\right\}^2\right]
\le \|h\|_\infty^2 \Lambda_{0,\ell,0}(\tau)
\int_0^{\tau}E\{D_n(u)^2\}d\Lambda_{0,\ell,0}(u).
\]
The integral on the right is $O(n^{-1})$ by
\eqref{eq:cox-risk-mean-first-moment} and \eqref{eq:cox-risk-mean-second-moment},
since $\int s_0d\Lambda_{0,\ell,0}$ and $\Lambda_{0,\ell,0}(\tau)$ are finite. Thus the second moment of the
integral in \eqref{eq:cox-risk-mean-replacement} is $O(n^{-1})$, as required.

label: lem:breslow-weighted-linearization
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:breslow-weighted-linearization}
Fix a transition $\ell=(j,k)$, write $s_{\ell,0}(u)=s_\ell^{(0)}(\beta_{\ell,0},u)$,
and let $h_\ell$ be a bounded deterministic function.  Under
Assumption~\ref{ass:cox-main-primitives},
\begin{align}
\label{eq:breslow-weighted-linearization}
&\int_0^{\tau}s_{\ell,0}(u)h_\ell(u)
\,d\{\widehat\Lambda_{0,\ell}-\Lambda_{0,\ell,0}\}(u) \\
&\qquad=
\int_0^{\tau}h_\ell(u)\,d\bar M_{\ell,0}^{\beta}(u)
-
B_{\ell,h}^{\top}(\widehat\beta_\ell-\beta_{\ell,0})
+O_p(n^{-1}), \notag
\end{align}
where $d\bar M_{\ell,0}^{\beta}$ is the training-average Cox martingale
increment defined in \eqref{eq:cox-average-martingale},
and
$B_{\ell,h} =\int_0^{\tau}s_{\ell,0}(u)h_\ell(u) \bar z_\ell(\beta_{\ell,0},u)\,d\Lambda_{0,\ell,0}(u)$.
Consequently the left side is $O_p(n^{-1/2})$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $\beta_0=\beta_{\ell,0}$, $\widehat\beta=\widehat\beta_\ell$, $S_n(\beta,u)=S_{\ell,n}^{(0)}(\beta,u)$, $s_0=s_{\ell,0}$, and $J=J_{\ell,n}$. The Breslow
definition and the decomposition $\mathbb P_{\mathrm{tr},n} dN_\ell=d\bar M_{\ell,0}^{\beta}+S_n(\beta_0,u)d\Lambda_{0,\ell,0}$ give
\begin{align*}
\int s_0h\,d(\widehat\Lambda_0-\Lambda_0)
&=R_{1,n}+R_{2,n}+R_{3,n}, \\
R_{1,n}&=\int h\,d\bar M_{\ell,0}^{\beta}, \\
R_{2,n}&=\int h\left\{\frac{s_0J}{S_n(\widehat\beta)}-1\right\}d\bar M_{\ell,0}^{\beta}, \\
R_{3,n}&=\int s_0h\left\{\frac{JS_n(\beta_0)}{S_n(\widehat\beta)}-1\right\}
 d\Lambda_{0,\ell,0}.
\end{align*}
For $R_{2,n}$, write

\[
\begin{aligned}
R_{2,n}&=\int h\left\{\frac{s_0J}{S_n(\beta_0)}-1\right\}d\bar M_{\ell,0}^{\beta}\\
&\quad+\int h\left\{\frac{s_0J}{S_n(\widehat\beta)}-\frac{s_0J}{S_n(\beta_0)}\right\} d\bar M_{\ell,0}^{\beta}.
\end{aligned}
\]

The first term has a predictable integrand and expected quadratic
variation bounded by

\[
\frac{\|h\|_\infty^2}{n}\int E\left[ S_n(\beta_0,u)\left\{\frac{s_0(u)J(u)}{S_n(\beta_0,u)}-1\right\}^2 \right]d\Lambda_{0,\ell,0}(u)=O(n^{-2})
\]

using \eqref{eq:cox-denominator-ratio}; hence it is $O_p(n^{-1})$.
The second contains the random parameter $\widehat\beta$. On $\|\widehat\beta-\beta_0\|\le Mn^{-1/2}$,
Lemma~\ref{lem:cox-self-normalized-equicontinuity} bounds it by $O_p(n^{-1})$.
Since this event has probability tending to one by
Lemma~\ref{lem:cox-root-consistency}, $R_{2,n}=O_p(n^{-1})$.

For $R_{3,n}$, the indicator $J$ does not depend on $\beta$.
On $\|\widehat\beta-\beta_0\|\le1$, Taylor expansion of $S_n(\beta_0,u)/S_n(\widehat\beta,u)$ on $\{J=1\}$ gives
\[
\frac{S_n(\beta_0,u)}{S_n(\widehat\beta,u)}-1
= -\bar Z_{\ell,n}(\beta_0,u)^\top(\widehat\beta-\beta_0)+\rho_n(u),
\qquad
|\rho_n(u)|\le C\|\widehat\beta-\beta_0\|^2.
\]
The contribution from $\{J=0\}$ has expectation bounded by $Cn^{-1}\int \mathbf 1\{s_0>0\}s_0(u)^{-1}d\Lambda_{0,\ell,0}(u)$ and
is therefore $O_p(n^{-1})$. Since $\|\widehat\beta-\beta_0\|^2=O_p(n^{-1})$ and $\int s_0d\Lambda_{0,\ell,0}<\infty$, the Taylor remainder
contributes $O_p(n^{-1})$. Thus
\[
R_{3,n}=-(\widehat\beta-\beta_0)^\top
\int s_0(u)h(u)\bar Z_{\ell,n}(\beta_0,u)d\Lambda_{0,\ell,0}(u)+O_p(n^{-1}).
\]
Lemma~\ref{lem:cox-risk-mean-replacement} replaces $\bar Z_{\ell,n}$ in this
integral by $\bar z_\ell$ with error $O_p(n^{-1/2})$. Multiplication by $\|\widehat\beta-\beta_0\|=O_p(n^{-1/2})$
makes this error $O_p(n^{-1})$, so $R_{3,n}=-B_{\ell,h}^\top(\widehat\beta-\beta_0)+O_p(n^{-1})$. Combining the three terms proves
\eqref{eq:breslow-weighted-linearization}.

The leading martingale $R_{1,n}$ has expected quadratic variation bounded
by $n^{-1}\|h\|_\infty^2\int s_0d\Lambda_{0,\ell,0}$ and is consequently $O_p(n^{-1/2})$. The coefficient-estimation term
is also $O_p(n^{-1/2})$.

label: lem:cox-row-stabilization
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Lemmas~\ref{lem:breslow-rates} and~\ref{lem:cox-root-consistency}
give the raw-hazard bound
$\sup_x\|\bar A_n(\cdot\mid x)-A_0(\cdot\mid x)\|_{\infty,\tau}=O_p(n^{-1/2}).$
Indeed, on the localization event of Lemma~\ref{lem:cox-root-consistency},
bounded covariates imply
$|e^{\widehat\beta_\ell^\top x}-e^{\beta_{\ell,0}^\top x}| \le C\|\widehat\beta_\ell-\beta_{\ell,0}\|, \qquad \sup_x e^{\widehat\beta_\ell^\top x}\le C$
The squared-jump bound \eqref{eq:breslow-squared-jumps} likewise gives
$\sup_x\sum_u\{\Delta\bar A_{\ell,n}(u\mid x)\}^2=O_p(n^{-1}).$
Continuity of $A_0$ makes this also the squared-jump bound for the raw
hazard error.

The row transformation is pathwise admissible: the nonnegative row-zero
increments sum to $1-e^{-x_0}\le1$, and the row-one increment is $1-e^{-x_{12}}\le1$.
Hence $\widehat A_n(\cdot\mid x)\in\mathscr A_{\tau}$. To bound the correction $\widehat A_n-\bar A_n$ in total variation,
fix $u$ and write the raw row-zero increments as
$x_{01}=\Delta\bar A_{01,n}(u\mid x)$, $x_{02}=\Delta\bar A_{02,n}(u\mid x)$, $x_0=x_{01}+x_{02}$.
The transformed increments are
$\Delta\widehat A_{0k,n}(u\mid x) =\frac{x_{0k}}{x_0}\{1-e^{-x_0}\}, \qquad k=1,2,$
with value zero when $x_0=0$. The inequality $|1-e^{-x}-x|\le x^2/2$ gives
$\left|\Delta\widehat A_{0k,n}(u\mid x)-x_{0k}\right| = x_{0k} \left|\frac{1-e^{-x_0}}{x_0}-1\right| \le x_{0k}x_0/2 \le x_0^2/2 .$
Summing over $k=1,2$ and using $(x_{01}+x_{02})^2\le2x_{01}^2+2x_{02}^2$ bounds the row-zero contribution
by a constant times $x_{01}^2+x_{02}^2$. For row one, set $x_{12}=\Delta\bar A_{12,n}(u\mid x)$; then
$|\Delta\widehat A_{12,n}(u\mid x)-x_{12}| =|1-e^{-x_{12}}-x_{12}| \le x_{12}^2/2.$
Summing over the empirical jump times yields
\[
\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal J}\sup_x
\left|\widehat A_{\ell,n}(\cdot\mid x)-\bar A_{\ell,n}(\cdot\mid x)\right|_{\mathrm{TV},\tau}
\le C\sup_x\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal J}\sum_{0<u\le\tau}
\{\Delta\bar A_{\ell,n}(u\mid x)\}^2
=O_p(n^{-1}),
\]
The final equality follows from \eqref{eq:breslow-squared-jumps},
transferred to the conditional hazards by bounded covariates. The sup-norm
correction is therefore also $O_p(n^{-1})$. Finally,
$|\Delta\widehat A_{\ell,n}|\le |\Delta\bar A_{\ell,n}|+C(\Delta\bar A_{\ell,n})^2$
and the raw squared-jump bound give the corresponding bound for the
transformed hazards. This proves \eqref{eq:cox-conditional-hazard-sup},
\eqref{eq:cox-conditional-hazard-jumps}, and \eqref{eq:cox-row-stabilization-variation}.

label: thm:cox-breslow-rates
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The coefficient and baseline-hazard rates stated in
Proposition~\ref{prop:cox-main-regime} follow, for the estimators specified
here, from Lemmas~\ref{lem:cox-root-consistency}
and~\ref{lem:breslow-rates}.
Lemma~\ref{lem:breslow-weighted-linearization} gives
\eqref{eq:cox-source-weighted-rate}: its leading martingale has order
$n^{-1/2}$, the coefficient-estimation term is $O_p(n^{-1/2})$, and the remainder
is $O_p(n^{-1})$.

By Lemma~\ref{lem:cox-row-stabilization}, $\widehat A_n(\cdot\mid x)\in\mathscr A_{\tau}$ for every $x$.
Lemma~\ref{lem:cox-row-stabilization} gives
$\sup_x\|\widehat A_n(\cdot\mid x)-A_0(\cdot\mid x)\|_{\infty,\tau} =O_p(n^{-1/2}).$
Its proof obtains this rate for the raw hazards and transfers it to the
row-admissible hazards using the $O_p(n^{-1})$ total-variation correction in
\eqref{eq:cox-row-stabilization-variation}.

The true hazards satisfy
$\sup_x A_{\ell,0}(\tau\mid x) \le e^{\|\beta_{\ell,0}\|K}\Lambda_{0,\ell,0}(\tau)<\infty.$
For the fitted hazards, Lemma~\ref{lem:breslow-rates} gives
$\widehat\Lambda_{0,\ell}(\tau)=O_p(1)$. Bounded covariates and $\widehat\beta_\ell=\beta_{\ell,0}+O_p(n^{-1/2})$ imply $\sup_x e^{\widehat\beta_\ell^\top x}=O_p(1)$. Row stabilization
changes the total mass by at most the $O_p(n^{-1})$ total-variation correction.
Thus, for each $\eta>0$, there exists $M_\eta<\infty$ such that
$\Pr\left( \sup_x |A_0(\cdot\mid x)|_{\tau} \vee \sup_x |\widehat A_n(\cdot\mid x)|_{\tau} \le M_\eta \right)\ge1-\eta$
for sufficiently large $n$.
On this event, \eqref{eq:product-integral-lipschitz} in
Lemma~\ref{lem:product-integral-expansion} gives
\[
\sup_x\kappa_{\mathrm{PI}}\{A_0(\cdot\mid x),\widehat A_n(\cdot\mid x)\}
\le
C_{\mathrm{PI}}(M_\eta,\tau)
\sup_x\|\widehat A_n(\cdot\mid x)-A_0(\cdot\mid x)\|_{\infty,\tau}.
\]
The conditional-hazard rate above makes the right-hand side $O_p(n^{-1/2})$.
Applying \eqref{eq:rmst-product-integral-bound} in
Lemma~\ref{lem:rmst-hazard-derivative} yields
\[
\sup_x|\mu_{\widehat A_n}(\tau\mid x)-\mu_{A_0}(\tau\mid x)|
\le 2\tau
\sup_x\kappa_{\mathrm{PI}}\{A_0(\cdot\mid x),\widehat A_n(\cdot\mid x)\}
=O_p(n^{-1/2}).
\]
and in particular
$P_X\{\mu_{\widehat A_n}(\tau\mid X)-\mu_{A_0}(\tau\mid X)\} =O_p(n^{-1/2}).$

Adding and subtracting the evaluation and population means gives
\[
\widehat\mu_{n,m}^{\mathrm{plug}}-\mu_\tau(A_0)
=(\mathbb P_{\mathrm{ev},m}-P_X)\mu_{A_0}
+P_X(\mu_{\widehat A_n}-\mu_{A_0})
+(\mathbb P_{\mathrm{ev},m}-P_X)(\mu_{\widehat A_n}-\mu_{A_0})
\]
The first term is $O_p(m^{-1/2})$ by boundedness of $\mu_{A_0}$,
and the second is $O_p(n^{-1/2})$ by the preceding uniform bound.
For the last term, conditional independence and
\eqref{eq:conditional-evaluation-variance} give a variance bounded by
$m^{-1}P_X(\mu_{\widehat A_n}-\mu_{A_0})^2=O_p(m^{-1}n^{-1})$.
Conditional Chebyshev's inequality proves
\eqref{eq:cox-plugin-rate}; the stated special case follows when $m\asymp n$.

label: lem:cox-rmst-source-domination
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:cox-rmst-source-domination}
Let
$L_{01}(u,x)=p_0(u-\mid x)\{V_{1,0}(u,\tau\mid x)-V_{0,0}(u,\tau\mid x)\},$
$L_{02}(u,x)=-p_0(u-\mid x)V_{0,0}(u,\tau\mid x)$, $L_{12}(u,x)=-p_1(u-\mid x)V_{1,0}(u,\tau\mid x)$.
For $r=0,1,\ldots,d$, with $Z_0\equiv1$, define
$a_{\ell,r}(u)=P_X\{L_\ell(u,X)e^{\beta_{\ell,0}^\top X}Z_r\}$, $s_{\ell,0}(u)=E\{Y_{j(\ell)}(u)e^{\beta_{\ell,0}^\top X}\}$.
Under conditional independent censoring with $\inf_{u,x}G(u-\mid x)\ge g_0>0$,
there are bounded deterministic functions $h_{\ell,r}$ such that
$a_{\ell,r}(u)=s_{\ell,0}(u)h_{\ell,r}(u)$, and $\|h_{\ell,r}\|_\infty\le K_r\tau/g_0,$
where $K_0=1$ and $K_r=K$ for $r\ge1$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For $\ell=(j,k)$, the bound $|L_\ell(u,x)|\le\tau p_j(u-\mid x)$ gives
$|a_{\ell,r}(u)| \le K_r\tau P_X\{p_j(u-\mid X)e^{\beta_{\ell,0}^\top X}\}.$
Conditional independent censoring implies
\[
s_{\ell,0}(u)=P_X\{p_j(u-\mid X)G(u-\mid X)e^{\beta_{\ell,0}^\top X}\}
\ge g_0P_X\{p_j(u-\mid X)e^{\beta_{\ell,0}^\top X}\}.
\]
Consequently, $|a_{\ell,r}(u)|\le K_r\tau g_0^{-1}s_{\ell,0}(u)$.
Taking $h_{\ell,r}=a_{\ell,r}/s_{\ell,0}$ on $\{s_{\ell,0}>0\}$ and zero elsewhere
proves the assertion.

label: eq:cox-rmst-taylor-expansion
title: Proof
body_md:
Lemma~\ref{lem:rmst-hazard-derivative} gives
$\dot\mu_{\tau,A_0}[\widehat A_n-A_0](x) =\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal J}\int_0^{\tau}L_\ell(u,x) \,d\{\widehat A_{\ell,n}-A_{\ell,0}\}(u\mid x).$
We first treat the raw Cox hazards $\bar A_n$ and then account for the
row-stabilized hazards $\widehat A_n$. Fix $\ell$ and write $\Delta_\beta=\widehat\beta_\ell-\beta_{\ell,0}$.
For bounded $x$, Taylor's formula gives
\begin{align}
\label{eq:cox-rmst-taylor-expansion}
&\int L_\ell(u,x)\,d\{\bar A_{\ell,n}-A_{\ell,0}\}(u\mid x) \\
&=\int L_\ell(u,x)e^{\beta_{\ell,0}^\top x}
\,d\{\widehat\Lambda_{0,\ell}-\Lambda_{0,\ell,0}\}(u) \notag \\
&\quad+\Delta_\beta^\top
\int L_\ell(u,x)e^{\beta_{\ell,0}^\top x}x\,d\Lambda_{0,\ell,0}(u) \notag \\
&\quad+\Delta_\beta^\top
\int L_\ell(u,x)e^{\beta_{\ell,0}^\top x}x\,
   d\{\widehat\Lambda_{0,\ell}-\Lambda_{0,\ell,0}\}(u)
+R_{\ell,n}(x). \notag
\end{align}
The last line retains the product of the regression and baseline-hazard
errors. The remaining Taylor term satisfies
$P_X|R_{\ell,n}(X)|=O_p(n^{-1}).$
Indeed, the second derivative of $e^{\beta^\top x}$ is uniformly bounded on the
local-root event, giving
$$|R_{\ell,n}(x)|\le C\|\Delta_\beta\|^2 \left\{\Lambda_{0,\ell,0}(\tau)+ \sup_{t\le\tau}|\widehat\Lambda_{0,\ell}(t)-\Lambda_{0,\ell,0}(t)|\right\}.$$
By Lemmas~\ref{lem:cox-root-consistency} and~\ref{lem:breslow-rates},
the right-hand side is $O_p(n^{-1})$ after taking $P_X$-expectations.

The coefficient of the first baseline term is
$a_{\ell,0}(u)=P_X\{L_\ell(u,X)e^{\beta_{\ell,0}^\top X}\}$, obtained
by taking $P_X$-expectations in \eqref{eq:cox-rmst-taylor-expansion}.
Lemma~\ref{lem:cox-rmst-source-domination} gives $a_{\ell,0}(u)=s_{\ell,0}(u)h_{\ell,0}(u)$ with bounded
$h_{\ell,0}$.
Hence Lemma~\ref{lem:breslow-weighted-linearization} yields
$\int a_{\ell,0}(u)d\{\widehat\Lambda_{0,\ell}-\Lambda_{0,\ell,0}\}(u) =O_p(n^{-1/2})$.
The pure parameter term is therefore $O_p(n^{-1/2})$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:cox-root-consistency}.
with the finite vector coefficient
$\int P_X\{ L_\ell(u,X)e^{\beta_{\ell,0}^\top X}X\} d\Lambda_{0,\ell,0}(u)$.

For the cross term, the coordinate coefficients
$u_{\ell,r}(u)=P_X\{L_\ell(u,X)e^{\beta_{\ell,0}^\top X}Z_r\}$
satisfy $u_{\ell,r}(u)=s_{\ell,0}(u)h_{\ell,r}(u)$ with bounded $h_{\ell,r}$, again by
Lemma~\ref{lem:cox-rmst-source-domination}.
Thus Lemma~\ref{lem:breslow-weighted-linearization} gives
$\int u_{\ell,r}(u)d\{\widehat\Lambda_{0,\ell}-\Lambda_{0,\ell,0}\}(u) =O_p(n^{-1/2})$
for each $r$.
Fixed dimension and $\|\Delta_\beta\|=O_p(n^{-1/2})$ make the cross term $O_p(n^{-1})$.

Finally, replace $\bar A_n$ by $\widehat A_n$. The derivative coefficients satisfy
$|L_\ell(u,x)|\le\tau$, while \eqref{eq:cox-row-stabilization-variation} in
Lemma~\ref{lem:cox-row-stabilization} gives
$\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal J}\sup_x \left|\widehat A_{\ell,n}(\cdot\mid x)-\bar A_{\ell,n}(\cdot\mid x)\right|_{\mathrm{TV},\tau} =O_p(n^{-1})$.
Thus row stabilization changes $\dot\mu_{\tau,A_0}^{\mathrm{std}}[\cdot]$ by $O_p(n^{-1})$. Summing over the
three transitions proves \eqref{eq:cox-standardized-derivative-rate}.

title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:bounded-vs-subgaussian-cox}
The bounded-support assumption gives the uniform-in-$x$ conditional-hazard bound
used in Proposition~\ref{prop:cox-main-regime}.  On the local-root event,
$\|\widehat\beta_\ell-\beta_{\ell,0}\|=O_p(n^{-1/2})$, and bounded covariates imply
\[
\sup_x\|
\bar A_n(\cdot\mid x)-A_0(\cdot\mid x)\|_{\infty,\tau}
\le C\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal J}\left
\{\|\widehat\beta_\ell-\beta_{\ell,0}\|+
\sup_{t\le\tau}|\widehat\Lambda_{0,\ell}(t)-\Lambda_{0,\ell,0}(t)|\right\}
=O_p(n^{-1/2}).
\]
For fixed-dimensional sub-Gaussian covariates, the same argument gives the
integrated replacement
$P_X\left[\sup_{t\le\tau} |\bar A_{\ell,n}(t\mid X)-A_{\ell,0}(t\mid X)|^2\right]=O_p(n^{-1}),$
provided the corresponding exponential moments are finite.  The inverse-risk
condition \eqref{eq:cox-main-source-support} is needed in both formulations.

title: Proof
body_md:
Condition on the training sample and write $B=\widehat A_n$, $A=A_0$, and $D=B-A$.
The evaluation observations are then independent and identically distributed,
and
$\widehat\mu_{n,m}^{\textsf{os}}-\mu_\tau(A_0) =(\mathbb P_{\mathrm{ev},m}-P)\widehat\psi_n+B_n, \qquad B_n=P\widehat\psi_n-\mu_\tau(A_0).$
The true Doob--Meyer decomposition $dN_\ell=dM_{\ell,0}+Y_{j(\ell)}dA_{\ell,0}$ and the mean-zero property of
martingale integrals yield
\[
B_n=P_X\{\mu_B(\tau\mid X)-\mu_A(\tau\mid X)\}
+
\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal J}P\int_0^\tau
\widehat H_{\ell,n}(u,X)Y_{j(\ell)}(u)
\,d\{A_{\ell,0}-B_\ell\}(u\mid X).
\]
The first-order expansion at $A$ in Lemma~\ref{lem:rmst-hazard-derivative}
gives
\[
\mu_B(\tau\mid x)-\mu_A(\tau\mid x)
=
\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal J}\int_0^\tau
P^A_{j(\ell)}(u-\mid x)
\{V^A_{k(\ell)}-V^A_{j(\ell)}\}(u,\tau\mid x)
\,dD_\ell(u\mid x)+r_n(x),
\]
with $|r_n(x)|\le \tau\omega_{\rm PI}\{A(\cdot\mid x),B(\cdot\mid x)\}$. Conditional independent censoring implies $E\{Y_{j(\ell)}(u)\mid X=x\}=P^A_{j(\ell)}(0,u-\mid x)G(u-\mid x)$.
Substitution proves \eqref{eq:onestep-decomposition}--\eqref{eq:onestep-bias}.

For the censoring-only representation, start from the exact Duhamel identity
\[
P_B(0,t\mid x)-P_A(0,t\mid x)
=
\int_{(0,t]}P_A(0,u-\mid x)d\mathbf D(u\mid x)P_B(u,t\mid x).
\]
Multiplication by $a_{\mathrm{surv}}$, integration over $t\in[0,\tau]$, and Stieltjes--Fubini
give
\[
\mu_B(\tau\mid x)-\mu_A(\tau\mid x)
=
\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal J}\int_0^\tau
P^A_{j(\ell)}(u-\mid x)
\{V^B_{k(\ell)}-V^B_{j(\ell)}\}(u,\tau\mid x)
\,dD_\ell(u\mid x).
\]
The implemented hazard-induced weights use the same fitted law $B$ in
the fitted RMST, residual contrast, and compensator. Substitution therefore
gives \eqref{eq:onestep-censoring-bias}. When $\widehat G_n=G$, the factor in braces
in that identity vanishes, so $B_n=0$ for every bounded admissible fitted
transition law $B$.

label: eq:V-pvar-direct
title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $x$ and suppress it where unambiguous.
Duhamel's identity with the zero hazard triplet, row-stochasticity, and
$\|d\mathbf A(r)\|_\infty\le2\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal J}dA_\ell(r\mid x)$ give
$\|P_A(s,t)-I\|_\infty \le2\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal J}A_\ell((s,t]\mid x)$, $0\le s<t\le\tau$.
For a partition $0=t_0<\cdots<t_m=\tau$, set
$\Delta_r|A|=\sum_{\ell\in\mathcal J}A_\ell((t_{r-1},t_r]\mid x)$.
Splitting the integrals defining $V_j^A$ at $t_r$ and using
$P_A(t_{r-1},t)=P_A(t_{r-1},t_r)P_A(t_r,t)$ yields
\[
|V_j^A(t_r,\tau\mid x)-V_j^A(t_{r-1},\tau\mid x)|
\le t_r-t_{r-1}+2(\tau-t_r)\Delta_r|A|
\le t_r-t_{r-1}+2\tau\Delta_r|A|.
\]
Summing over the partition and taking the supremum gives
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:V-pvar-direct}
\max_{j=0,1}\operatorname{pvar}\{V_j^A(\cdot,\tau\mid x);[0,\tau]\}
\le\tau\{1+2|A(\cdot\mid x)|_\tau\}.
\end{equation}
Write $W_{01,A}=V_1^A-V_0^A$, $W_{02,A}=-V_0^A$, and
$W_{12,A}=-V_1^A$, so $H_{\ell,A}=W_{\ell,A}q_G$ with
$q_G(u,x)=G(u-\mid x)^{-1}$.
Then $\|W_{\ell,A}\|_\infty\le\tau$ and
$\operatorname{pvar}(W_{\ell,A})\le2\tau\{1+2|A(\cdot\mid x)|_\tau\}$.
Monotonicity and positivity of $G$ give
$\|q_G\|_\infty\le g_0^{-1}$ and $\operatorname{pvar}(q_G)\le g_0^{-1}$.
Applying
$\operatorname{pvar}(fg)\le\|f\|_\infty\operatorname{pvar}(g)+\|g\|_\infty\operatorname{pvar}(f)$
therefore yields
\[
\max_{\ell\in\mathcal J}\{\|H_{\ell,A}\|_\infty+\operatorname{pvar}(H_{\ell,A})\}
\le\frac{4\tau}{g_0}\{1+|A(\cdot\mid x)|_\tau\}.
\]
Finally, $\|Y_j\|_\infty\le1$ and $\operatorname{pvar}(Y_j)\le2$. The same
product-variation inequality gives
\[
\operatorname{pvar}(Y_jH_{\ell,A})+\|Y_jH_{\ell,A}\|_\infty
\le\operatorname{pvar}(H_{\ell,A})+3\|H_{\ell,A}\|_\infty
\le\frac{6\tau}{g_0}\{1+|A(\cdot\mid x)|_\tau\},
\]
proving \eqref{eq:rmst-weight-variation} and \eqref{eq:weighted-risk-variation}.
